# Testing

*6 of 79 rules below are **designed** rather than shipped, and are marked where they appear.*

<a id="testing-test-attribute"></a>

## A test is a method marked `#[Test]`, and its table is built while compiling

`rule:testing/test-attribute`

A test is an ordinary `public` method carrying `#[Test]`, on an ordinary class. There is no naming
convention, no base class to extend and no interface to implement: nothing about a test is inferred
from spelling.

The compiler collects every marked method into a table while it checks, keyed by class label, the
way the route table is built — so discovery costs nothing at startup, and five malformed shapes are
compile errors rather than tests that silently never run: two methods of one class sharing a name, a
`static` method, one returning anything but `void`, one that is not `public`, and one with no body.
The runner constructs the class and calls the member, so each of those is one question about what
shape a test method has, asked once. Each row also carries the span of its method's **name** — where every refusal
about that test already points — because that is the one fact about a test nothing downstream can
recompute, and it is what locates a test in a report and in an editor's test tree.

`#[Test]`'s payload is an options bag — `skip`, `at`, `seed`, `db`, `server`, `retries`,
`because`, `timeout` ([`testing/a-test-has-a-wall-time-limit`](testing.md#testing-a-test-has-a-wall-time-limit)) and `tags`
([`testing/tags-and-shards-select-what-runs`](testing.md#testing-tags-and-shards-select-what-runs)) — every field optional and every field checked at its own type. An option the roster does
not name is refused, one written twice is refused, and `skip: true` is a `bool` where a `string` is
declared.

The attribute is matched **nominally**, by resolved name: `#[Core\Test]` and a `use`d `#[Test]` are
one attribute, and a userland `class Test` is never it. The marker and the assertions are one class,
so a single `use Core\Test;` places both.

**Declined:**
- **A `test` keyword** (`test "a name is trimmed" { ... }`). It reads better, and it costs new
  grammar, a second scoping rule and a construct the formatter, the language server, the resilient
  parser and the converter must each learn, for a readability gain over a mechanism the route table
  already uses.
- **A `test*` naming convention.** The compiler reads no meaning out of spelling
  ([`core-api/identifier-casing`](core-api.md#core-api-identifier-casing)), and a method misspelled `tsetFoo` would silently be nothing.

<sub>See also [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test), [`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures), [`testing/data-rows`](testing.md#testing-data-rows), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict).</sub>

<a id="testing-tests-never-reach-a-build"></a>

## `nvs run` and `nvs build` lower no test, and `nvs check` type-checks every one

`rule:testing/tests-never-reach-a-build`

A `#[Test]` method may be declared in any file — beside the class it tests, or in a separate tree.
What makes a method a test is the attribute, never the path.

**Test code is a method that carries a testing marker:** `#[Test]`, `#[Fixture]`, `#[BeforeClass]`,
`#[AfterClass]` or `#[AfterEachTest]`. A data row is an attribute on a `#[Test]` method, and an
assertion message, a double and an anonymous function are written inside a test's body, so each of
them is test code with the method it belongs to. The class that declares them is not test code:
its constructor and its other methods are compiled as any class's are, because a class with a
`#[Test]` method may be the class under test as well.

`nvs test` compiles and runs test code. `nvs run`, the reload of a running program, and `nvs build`
do not lower it at all: no test method is compiled, and no class's method table names one. A built
artifact carries no test surface, and a run pays nothing for one. One program is therefore two
compiled units, and the artifact cache keys them apart, so neither command loads the other's.

**A call into test code from other code does not compile** (`E0889`). That covers a call, a method
reference and a class-reference call whose method resolves to test code, written anywhere but inside
test code. It is a compile error under every command, `nvs test` included, so a program compiles the
same way for a run and for its tests. Without it, a call into a test would check and then name a
function the build left out.

`nvs check` does type-check test code. That is the one place tests and non-tests are treated alike,
and deliberately so: a test cannot rot silently while the code around it changes.

**What it costs:** one set of test method labels per compile, O(test methods), and nothing at run
time.

**Declined:**

- *A test class is test code as a whole.* A class with a `#[Test]` method may be the class under
  test, so leaving the class out would leave production methods out of a build.

<sub>See also [`testing/test-attribute`](testing.md#testing-test-attribute), [`testing/determinism-declared-on-the-test`](testing.md#testing-determinism-declared-on-the-test).</sub>

<a id="testing-isolate-per-test"></a>

## Every test runs in its own isolate and shares nothing but compiled code with its siblings

`rule:testing/isolate-per-test`

Each test runs on an isolate of its own: it shares compiled code with its siblings and nothing
else — not a static, not a cache entry, not an open handle. A static one test increments reads its
declared initial value in the next, always, with no flag to change it
([`statements/an-isolate-has-its-own-statics`](statements.md#statements-an-isolate-has-its-own-statics)).

This is not a hardening measure bolted onto a sequential runner; it is what makes a parallel one
possible at all, because an isolate is cheap enough to be the default rather than a per-case escape
hatch. Two consequences follow and are answered elsewhere: shared expensive setup needs its own
mechanism ([`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures)), and execution order carries no meaning, so the report is in
declaration order regardless of what finished when ([`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict)).

Each test isolate spends its parent's budget, so a suite has the same enforceable ceiling on memory
and CPU that a request has, and a runaway test is terminated rather than left to consume the
machine.

- **Memory:** each test in flight holds one isolate, one copy of each fixture it declares and one
  ledger entry per assertion it executes, all released when it joins. That is O(tests running), not
  O(tests in the suite): a suite of any size costs at one instant what its running tests cost.

**Declined:**
- **One isolate per test class.** It is cheaper and familiar, and it restores exactly the ordering
  dependence between cases that makes real suites flaky. Fixtures recover the setup cost it would
  save without the coupling ([`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures)).

<sub>See also [`testing/test-attribute`](testing.md#testing-test-attribute), [`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict), [`statements/an-isolate-has-its-own-statics`](statements.md#statements-an-isolate-has-its-own-statics).</sub>

<a id="testing-private-in-the-same-file"></a>

## A test reaches `private` members of classes declared in its own file, and nowhere else

`rule:testing/private-in-the-same-file`

A test method may reach `private` and `protected` members of classes declared **in the same file**.
A test in a separate file is held to the public contract.

This is the narrowest rule that avoids the failure it exists to prevent: a `public` method that
exists only because a test needed to reach it. White-box testing stays possible where the author has
already chosen to put the test next to the code; everything at a distance tests behaviour.

**A test method is test code** in [`testing/tests-never-reach-a-build`](testing.md#testing-tests-never-reach-a-build)'s sense: a method that
carries `#[Test]`, `#[Fixture]`, `#[BeforeClass]`, `#[AfterClass]` or `#[AfterEachTest]`, and every
anonymous function written inside one. A fixture builds what a test reaches, so it is admitted on the
same terms. Any other method of a test class is held to the ordinary levels, so a helper that reads a
`private` member has to be test code itself.

**The file is the one that declares the member's class**, read off that class's declaration. A test
class that `extends` the class from another file reaches its `protected` members the ordinary way and
nothing more.

**It costs nothing on the request path.** The admission is decided at compile time, in
`crates/nvs-types/src/signatures.rs`'s `is_visible_here`, and test code never reaches a build, so no
request can call a method that used it.

**Declined:** an attribute such as `#[VisibleForTesting]` on the member. It moves the decision to
the class under test, and the member is then reachable from every test anywhere.

<sub>See also [`testing/test-attribute`](testing.md#testing-test-attribute), [`testing/tests-never-reach-a-build`](testing.md#testing-tests-never-reach-a-build).</sub>

<a id="testing-assertions-are-typed"></a>

## An assertion names its subject first and compares two values of one type

`rule:testing/assertions-are-typed`

The assertion surface is static members on `Core\Test`, each taking its **subject first**:
`assertEquals($actual, $expected)`, with one trailing options shape, nothing mutating and failure
throwing. Both operands of an equality member are one type variable, so comparing an `int` against a
`string` does not compile. Because reversing the two is the commonest mistake in the ecosystem this
language is migrated from, every failure report labels the sides by name rather than by position, so
a reversed call still reads correctly.

Three equality members, and which one was asked for is visible at the call site. `assertSame` is
identity. `assertEquals` compares values — scalars natively, objects only through `Comparable`.
`assertEqualsDeep` is an explicit structural walk of properties, arrays and shapes, with a diff.
`assertEquals` on an object with no `compareTo` names `assertEqualsDeep` rather than falling back to
a property walk: a comparison that quietly changes meaning when a class gains a field is a bug found
years later.

`assertThrows`'s second argument is a `C::class` written at the call, and `C` is a class of the
`Throwable` tree (`E0865`). A string, a variable and a class outside the tree do not compile: a
misspelt name would otherwise fail only when the test runs, and a class nothing throws makes an
assertion that can never pass. The parameter stays a `string`, since `C::class` is one
([`types/class-reference`](types.md#types-class-reference)), so the check is made at the argument.

The roster is wide on purpose. Ranking the right member by the subject's type at the call site is
the language server's job, and not a reason to reshape the API into a chain.

**Declined:**
- **A fluent matcher chain** (`Core\Test::that($actual)->equals($expected)`). A chain's one
  advantage over a static roster is matchers scoped to the subject's type, and that needs members
  that exist only at some instantiations of a generic class, which Novis does not have. Without it
  every matcher is declared for every subject, so `that(5)->startsWith("x")` checks the prefix and
  not the subject: the chain type-checks strictly less than the roster, and also costs a builder and
  a second shape unlike every other `Core` member. Only member specialization would reopen it, never
  the roster's size.
- **Static members for scalars beside a per-kind assertion class for collections.** It does scope
  its matchers correctly, and it buys not repeating the subject across consecutive lines at the cost
  of two ways to assert about an array and a boundary between them to defend forever. Each repeated
  line also carries its own failure location.

<sub>See also [`testing/failure-ledger`](testing.md#testing-failure-ledger), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict), [`testing/inline-snapshots`](testing.md#testing-inline-snapshots).</sub>

<a id="testing-failure-ledger"></a>

## A failed assertion is a catchable `Throwable` and a ledger entry the test cannot erase

`rule:testing/failure-ledger`

`Core\Test\Failure` is an ordinary `Throwable`, and catching one is not merely allowed but
necessary: a composite assertion, a retry wrapper, a soft-assert block and any test *of* an
assertion all need to intercept one.

Every assertion **also** records its outcome into a per-test ledger the test's own code cannot
reach, and the runner reads the ledger rather than the exception state. A body that swallowed its
own failure with `catch (Throwable)` has still failed. There is deliberately no member that reads
the ledger back — that would hand the test the eraser this rule takes away — and the single throw
site records the entry *before* it hands the throw back, so no edge exists on which the throw
happened and the record did not.

`Core\Test::expectFailure(callable)` is the one greppable spelling for a failure consumed on
purpose: it runs the body, requires that it fail, and removes that entry. It decides from the ledger
rather than from what came back, so a body that caught its own failure has still failed; a body in
which nothing failed is itself a failure; and the passing assertions inside a discharged body stay,
because they really ran.

**Declined:**
- **A failure that escalates past `catch`.** It is the strongest guarantee, and it makes a
  user-written assertion helper, a retry wrapper and a soft-assert block impossible to express. The
  ledger gives the same guarantee without that loss.

<sub>See also [`testing/assertions-are-typed`](testing.md#testing-assertions-are-typed), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict), [`errors/throwable-hierarchy`](errors.md#errors-throwable-hierarchy).</sub>

<a id="testing-constructor-is-setup"></a>

## The constructor is the test's setup, and there is no second before-hook

`rule:testing/constructor-is-setup`

The constructor is the test's setup, and a stronger one than a `setUp` method can be: definite
property initialization guarantees every property is assigned before any test body runs. There is no
`#[BeforeEachTest]`, because the constructor is that hook. Cleanup after each test is
[`testing/after-each-test`](testing.md#testing-after-each-test), and setup and cleanup done once around a whole class are
[`testing/class-hooks`](testing.md#testing-class-hooks).

A test class's constructor therefore declares no parameters. One that does is reported as that test
failing rather than pretended past: the runner constructs the class with no arguments, and a test
method's own parameters are filled by [`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures) and [`testing/data-rows`](testing.md#testing-data-rows) instead.

<sub>See also [`testing/after-each-test`](testing.md#testing-after-each-test), [`testing/class-hooks`](testing.md#testing-class-hooks), [`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures), [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test).</sub>

<a id="testing-after-each-test"></a>

## `#[AfterEachTest]` runs on each attempt's own object, and is told which test ran and how it ended

`rule:testing/after-each-test`

`#[AfterEachTest]` marks a `public` instance method returning `void`, and the runner calls it on the
same object the test ran on, inside that test's isolate, after every attempt, whether the attempt
passed or failed. It exists for residue that outlives the isolate — a file, a row, a remote object.
Everything else needs no teardown: the isolate dies and takes everything inside it with it.

The hook knows which test ran because it runs on that test's own `$this`: whatever the constructor and
the test stored there is what it cleans up. It may also declare one parameter of type
`Core\Test\Outcome`, filled by type the way a fixture fills a test's parameter. It is a `Core` instance,
so it is read through methods:

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `class()` | the test class's name |
| `name()` | the method's name, with `#N` for a `#[TestWith]` row ([`testing/data-rows`](testing.md#testing-data-rows)) |
| `attempt()` | `1` for the first run, one more for each retry ([`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict)) |
| `passed()` | whether this attempt passed |
| `failures()` | the messages the report prints for this attempt, empty when it passed |

`Outcome` is for deciding what to keep and what to report — the evidence of a failed test kept under
its own name, the rest deleted. Cleanup that only one test needs belongs in that test's own `finally`,
not in a hook that branches on `$outcome->name()`. Any other parameter, or a second one, is refused where
it is written.

A retry is a fresh instance in the same isolate, so each attempt gets its own call on its own object.
A skipped test is never constructed, so the hook does not run for it. A constructor that throws leaves no object, so the hook does not run and the test fails with the
constructor's error. A hook that throws fails that attempt, and its failure is reported with the
test's own.

There is no `#[BeforeEachTest]`: the constructor is that hook ([`testing/constructor-is-setup`](testing.md#testing-constructor-is-setup)).

A test runs with the program's own grants (`crates/nvs-cli/src/runner.rs:409`), so the hook can remove
whatever the test was allowed to create.

A test that calls `exit()` is not followed by the hook, because nothing after an `exit()` runs
([`errors/escalation-ladder`](errors.md#errors-escalation-ladder)).

- **Memory:** one `Outcome` per attempt, a few strings and one list of failure messages, released when
  the hook returns. A class without the hook pays nothing.

**Declined:**
- **`#[After]`.** It does not say after what, beside `#[BeforeClass]` and `#[AfterClass]`
  ([`testing/class-hooks`](testing.md#testing-class-hooks)).
- **A static call such as `Test::current()`.** It would return a different value depending on runner
  state the method's signature does not show. A parameter is visible, optional and checked while
  compiling.
- **A `Throwable` in place of `failures`.** A test can fail several assertions and throw nothing, and
  the ledger already records each one as a message.

<sub>See also [`testing/constructor-is-setup`](testing.md#testing-constructor-is-setup), [`testing/class-hooks`](testing.md#testing-class-hooks), [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict).</sub>

<a id="testing-fixtures"></a>

## `#[Fixture]` is built once per class and injected into a test by the type it returns

`rule:testing/fixtures`

`#[Fixture]` marks a `public static` method, and what it supplies is its declared return type. It is
built **once per class**, in the parent, and reaches a test by that test declaring a parameter of
the type it returns. Resolution is by interned type and happens while compiling, so an unsatisfiable
parameter is a diagnostic naming the type it asked for rather than a null at run time. A fixture may
itself declare fixture parameters; a cycle is a compile error naming the whole chain.

Two fixtures of one class returning one type is a duplicate declaration, because resolution is by
type and two answers to one parameter is exactly the ambiguity that refusal prevents. Four
declarations cannot supply a value and are refused where they are written: one that is not `static`,
one that is not `public`, one returning `void`, and a method carrying both this marker and `#[Test]`.

Only a fixture that a test which will actually run asks for is built — a skipped test's fixture is
setup nobody wanted. Resolution runs once the whole class is collected rather than as the walk
descends, because a test may be written above the fixture that supplies it.

- **Memory:** a class's built fixtures are held from before its first test to after its last, and
  each test that declares one holds its own copy of it, made with the one graph copy `spawn` uses,
  for that test's life. A suite whose copies come to dominate its cost is answered by a copy-on-write
  path for immutable fixtures, measured first, never by sharing an isolate between tests.

<sub>See also [`testing/data-rows`](testing.md#testing-data-rows), [`testing/constructor-is-setup`](testing.md#testing-constructor-is-setup), [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test).</sub>

<a id="testing-class-hooks"></a>

## `#[BeforeClass]` and `#[AfterClass]` run once around a class's tests, and the second runs whenever the first started

`rule:testing/class-hooks`

`#[BeforeClass]` and `#[AfterClass]` mark `public static` methods returning `void` that run once
around a test class's tests, in the parent, and `#[AfterClass]` runs whenever `#[BeforeClass]` started.
They are for setup whose effect lives outside every isolate — a database created, its schema built and
its rows seeded once for the class, then dropped after its last test.

The order for one class is `#[BeforeClass]`, then the fixtures its selected tests need
([`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures)), then the tests, then `#[AfterClass]`. A fixture therefore reads what the setup
wrote. Neither hook runs for a class none of whose tests is selected, for the reason a fixture is not
built for one (`crates/nvs-cli/src/runner.rs:890`).

| What happens | Result |
|---|---|
| a test fails | `#[AfterClass]` still runs |
| `#[BeforeClass]` throws | no test runs, each selected test is reported failed with that error, and `#[AfterClass]` runs, because a setup that stopped halfway left something to remove |
| `#[AfterClass]` throws | the run fails, and the failure is reported against the class rather than a test |
| a test calls `exit()` or the process is killed | nothing after it runs ([`errors/escalation-ladder`](errors.md#errors-escalation-ladder)) |

`#[BeforeClass]` takes no parameter. `#[AfterClass]` may declare one of type `Core\Test\Summary`, filled
by type. It is a `Core` instance, so it is read through methods: `class()`, the counts `passed()`,
`failed()`, `flaky()` and `skipped()`, and `failedTests()`, the names of the failed tests as the report
prints them. A hook that keeps the database when `failed()` is above zero and drops it otherwise is the
case it exists for.

This order is the whole of what the runner guarantees. Classes run at the same time
([`testing/tests-run-across-every-core`](testing.md#testing-tests-run-across-every-core)), so two classes whose setups touch one database keep
apart themselves, for instance by naming the database after the class.

Tests of one class share what the setup wrote, so a test that writes to it runs under
`#[Test(db:)]` ([`testing/db-transaction`](testing.md#testing-db-transaction)). Without that, one test's rows reach the next and the
order of the tests matters again, which is what an isolate per test exists to prevent
([`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test)).

A hook that writes a static property in its own body is refused where it is written. Every test runs
in its own isolate and reads the static's declared initial value, so the write would look like setup
and set up nothing.

The fixtures are released before `#[AfterClass]` runs, so the hook can remove what a fixture held open.
A failed `#[AfterClass]` is printed under its class; a machine format writes it to stderr, and the run
exits with a failure either way.

- **Memory:** one `Summary` per class, four integers and the names of its failed tests, held in the
  parent from the class's first test to the return of `#[AfterClass]`. A class without the hooks pays
  nothing.

**Declined:**
- **A database setup written as a fixture.** A fixture is built only when a test declares its type, so
  a setup that returns nothing would never run, and a fixture has no cleanup.
- **A `#[BeforeClass]` that returns a value.** A value the tests receive is a fixture.
- **`#[BeforeAllTests]` and `#[AfterAllTests]`.** In a run of many classes, "all tests" reads as the
  whole run. `Class` names the scope.

<sub>See also [`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures), [`testing/after-each-test`](testing.md#testing-after-each-test), [`testing/db-transaction`](testing.md#testing-db-transaction), [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test), [`testing/tests-run-across-every-core`](testing.md#testing-tests-run-across-every-core).</sub>

<a id="testing-hook-inheritance"></a>

## A test class has at most one hook of each kind, and a subclass inherits hooks, fixtures and tests like any method

`rule:testing/hook-inheritance`

A test class has at most one `#[BeforeClass]`, one `#[AfterClass]` and one `#[AfterEachTest]`, and a
subclass inherits each of them, each `#[Fixture]`, each `#[Test]` and each `#[Property]` the way it
inherits any method. A base class's hook is therefore a default: a subclass that declares nothing runs
it, around its own tests.

| The subclass | Result |
|---|---|
| declares nothing | the inherited hook runs for the subclass |
| overrides the method by name | the override is the hook, and calls `parent::` to keep the base's steps |
| overrides with an empty body | the hook does nothing for that subclass |
| declares a second hook of that kind under another name | refused, naming both methods: two hooks of one kind on one class |
| overrides without repeating the attribute | refused, naming the method it overrides |

The override repeats the attribute so that a reader of the subclass alone sees that the method runs
around its tests. "Once per class" means once per test class: two subclasses of one base each run the
inherited `#[BeforeClass]` once, around their own tests, and an abstract base with no tests runs
nothing.

Fixtures, tests and properties follow the same table. A subclass's test receives an inherited fixture
by its type, an override by name replaces it, and a second fixture of the same type under another name
is the duplicate [`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures) already refuses. Each subclass runs every `#[Test]` and
`#[Property]` it inherits, around its own hooks and with its own fixtures, and reports it under its own
name, so `ShopTest` running a test written in `DatabaseTest` reports `ShopTest::itConnects`. One
contract test written once in a base class then runs against every implementation. A base class that is
not abstract is a test class of its own as well, and runs its tests once for itself.

**Declined:**
- **Several hooks of one kind, run in declaration order.** The order would be a rule every reader must
  know and no line of the code shows. A failure in the second of two setups would also need each setup
  paired with its own cleanup. Several steps go in the one method, in the order they are written.
- **Only the tests a class declares itself.** A base class could then share setup but not the tests
  that check it, and one contract test would have to be copied into every implementation's class.

<sub>See also [`testing/class-hooks`](testing.md#testing-class-hooks), [`testing/after-each-test`](testing.md#testing-after-each-test), [`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures).</sub>

<a id="testing-tests-run-across-every-core"></a>

## `nvs test` runs tests in parallel across every core, captures each test's output, and guarantees the hooks' order but not data consistency

`rule:testing/tests-run-across-every-core`

`nvs test` runs test isolates in parallel across every core, as many at once as `--jobs` allows, and
`--jobs` defaults to the machine's hardware threads as it already does for `.nvst` cases. Every test
already runs in an isolate of its own ([`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test)), so running them at once is a
scheduling question and not an isolation one. The runner places each test isolate with the placement a
program uses ([`concurrency/on-worker-runs-the-child-on-another-core`](concurrency.md#concurrency-on-worker-runs-the-child-on-another-core)), on cores the run starts for
itself: a test parks while its isolate runs, so the program under test and the script compiler are
installed once per core rather than once per test, where another test on that core would read them.
`--jobs 1` runs every test
on the runner's own core, one at a time. An extension host belongs to its thread, so each core installs
one of its own over the set the run loaded, and a program that calls an extension runs its tests in
parallel too. A test's calls run in its own request tree, under its own budget, and its instances end
with it, as a served request's do ([`packaging/a-guest-runs-under-the-requests-budget`](packaging.md#packaging-a-guest-runs-under-the-requests-budget)).

The runner guarantees order and nothing about data. The order it guarantees is the one
[`testing/class-hooks`](testing.md#testing-class-hooks) gives: `#[BeforeClass]` returns before the class's first test starts,
the class's fixtures are built before its first test, and `#[AfterClass]` starts after its last test has
finished. Tests of one class, and tests of different classes, run at the same time. What two of them
share outside their isolates, a database or a file, is the program's to keep apart.

The report is in declaration order, whatever order the tests finish in ([`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict)),
so a parallel run and a run on one core report the same thing. Coverage counts each test into a table
of its own and adds it to the run's when the test finishes, so the lines a test reached are still that
test's.

**A test's output is captured.** What a test, its hooks and its fixtures print while it runs is held for
that test. A test that passes discards it, and a test that fails prints it under its failure, in the
report's place for that test. What a class's `#[BeforeClass]` and fixtures print is held too, and
printed under the class's header whatever its tests did. `--show-output` turns capture off: output then
goes to the terminal as it is printed and is not attributed, so two tests running at once may mix their
lines. A test that reads the terminal reads end of input, so no test stops the run to wait for a person.

- **Memory:** each test in flight holds a parent context of its own, its isolate, its fixtures as bytes
  and as copies, its captured output and its own coverage table when coverage is on, all released when
  it is reported. A failed test's output is held until its report line is printed. That is O(`--jobs`),
  the most tests running at once, plus the results of finished tests waiting for an earlier one, and
  never the output of a test that passed. The run's cores are at most one thread per core, started
  with the first test placed and joined when the run ends.

**Declined:**
- **A second setting for the number of tests at once.** `--jobs` already says how many `.nvst` cases run
  at once, and a `#[Test]` run reads the same flag.
- **A runner that keeps two classes' data apart.** It would have to know what a test touches outside
  its isolate, and it cannot.
- **Output streamed by default.** Two tests running at once mix their lines, and a passing test's
  output is noise in every run.

<sub>See also [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test), [`testing/class-hooks`](testing.md#testing-class-hooks), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict), [`concurrency/on-worker-runs-the-child-on-another-core`](concurrency.md#concurrency-on-worker-runs-the-child-on-another-core).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-test-has-a-wall-time-limit"></a>

## `[limits] wall_time` bounds each test on its own, and `#[Test(timeout: ...)]` replaces it for one test

`rule:testing/a-test-has-a-wall-time-limit`

Each test runs under a wall-time limit: `[limits] wall_time` applies to every test on its own, and
`#[Test(timeout: "5s")]` replaces it for one test.

The limit is counted from the moment the test's class is constructed to the moment the test method
returns, so a test's fixtures and hooks count toward it and the tests that ran before it do not. A test
that passes its limit is stopped the way a request past its wall time is stopped
([`errors/on-limit`](errors.md#errors-on-limit)), and it fails with a message that names the limit and where it came from: the
configuration or the attribute. One limit covers every attempt of a test together, since the attempts
share the test's isolate ([`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict)): a test stopped at its limit is a failure,
and a retry gives it no new time.

`timeout` is written in the duration syntax `nvs.toml` uses, and a value that does not parse does not
compile, and neither does a zero. It may be longer or shorter than `[limits] wall_time`, and
`[limits.hard]`'s `wall_time` bounds it as it bounds a request's own `Core\Config::set`: a test whose
`timeout` is above that bound fails without running. Where neither is written, a test has no wall-time
limit, which is what `[limits] wall_time` already means when it is absent.

Reusing the request's key is the point: a test of a handler is held to the time the handler gets in
production, and one setting says it for both. The override is per test because a slow test is a fact
about that test, not about the run.

- **Memory:** one deadline per test in flight, the same one a request carries, and the thread `nvs run`
  times its own wall time with, for each test in flight that has a limit.

**Declined:**
- **A run-wide `--timeout` flag.** It is a second setting for what `[limits] wall_time` already says,
  and it would hold a fast test and a slow one to one number.
- **A default limit for tests when none is written.** A test that is meant to be slow would fail on a
  number nobody chose, and `nvs run` has no default either.

<sub>See also [`testing/test-attribute`](testing.md#testing-test-attribute), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict), [`errors/on-limit`](errors.md#errors-on-limit).</sub>

<a id="testing-tags-and-shards-select-what-runs"></a>

## `#[Test(tags: [...])]` labels a test, `--tag`/`--skip-tag` select by label, and `--shard N/M` runs one of M stable disjoint parts

`rule:testing/tags-and-shards-select-what-runs`

`#[Test(tags: ["slow", "db"])]` labels a test, `--tag` and `--skip-tag` select by label, and
`--shard N/M` runs the Nth of M disjoint parts of the selection.

A tag is a string, and a test may carry any number of them. `--tag slow` runs only the tests that carry
`slow`, and `--skip-tag slow` leaves them out. Both flags may be repeated: a test runs when it carries
at least one `--tag` label, or when no `--tag` is given, and when it carries no `--skip-tag` label. They
combine with `--filter`, and a test must pass every one. The compiler checks that each tag is a
non-empty string literal, and nothing more: the set of tags is the program's own. A `.nvst` case has no
tags, so `--tag` and `--skip-tag` beside a case tree are an error.

`--shard 2/4` splits the selected tests into four parts and runs the second. A test's part is a hash of
its `Class::method` name, a data row going with its test, so the parts do not change when another test
is added or removed, and four machines that each run one part run every selected test exactly once. A
`.nvst` case's part is a hash of its path. The parts are disjoint and together they are the whole
selection. They are not balanced by run time.

The summary says how many tests the selection left out, so a run that selected nothing is visible as
one. A `.nvst` run writes that count on its own line above the summary line, which stays the last.
The hash is FNV-1a over the name's bytes, with `/` between a path's parts on every platform, so every
machine of one CI run computes the same parts (`crates/nvs-test/src/shard.rs`).

- **Memory:** nothing per test beyond its list of tags, held in the test table while compiling.

**Declined:**
- **Shards balanced by recorded run time.** It needs a timing file every machine reads, and a part
  would change whenever the timings do, so two runs of one commit could split differently.
- **Shards by position in declaration order.** Adding one test would move every test after it to
  another part.
- **A closed list of tags declared somewhere.** A typo in a tag selects nothing, and the summary's count
  shows it. A roster would be a second place to edit for every new label.

<sub>See also [`testing/test-attribute`](testing.md#testing-test-attribute), [`testing/tests-run-across-every-core`](testing.md#testing-tests-run-across-every-core), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-run-can-stop-early-rerun-failures-and-shuffle"></a>

## `--fail-fast` stops starting tests after a failure, `--rerun-failed` runs the last run's failures, and `--shuffle` randomises start order with a printed seed

`rule:testing/a-run-can-stop-early-rerun-failures-and-shuffle`

`nvs test --fail-fast` stops starting tests after the first failure, `--rerun-failed` runs only the
tests the last run failed, and `--shuffle` starts tests in a random order and prints the seed.

**`--fail-fast`.** Once a failed test is reported, no new test starts, and no later class's
`#[BeforeClass]` runs. Tests already running finish and are reported, and the class whose test failed
still runs its `#[AfterClass]`. The summary counts the tests that never started as not run. Under
`--jobs 1` the run stops right after the first failure. With more jobs a failure is seen when it is
reported in declaration order, so a few more tests may start first. A flaky test is not a failure
([`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict)), so it does not stop the run. The exit status is the failed run's.

**`--rerun-failed`.** Every run of a program writes the `Class::label` of each failed test, a data
row's `#N` included, to `failed-tests/<hash>.txt` in the data folder, where the hash is of the
program's canonical entry path. `--rerun-failed` runs exactly those tests, and a later run overwrites
the file, with an empty one when nothing failed. When the last run failed nothing, or no run was
recorded, it runs the whole selection and says so in its first line. It combines with `--filter` and
the tag flags ([`testing/tags-and-shards-select-what-runs`](testing.md#testing-tags-and-shards-select-what-runs)), which narrow it further.

**`--shuffle`.** The tests of each class start in an order drawn from a seed, and the summary prints
the seed. `--shuffle=<seed>` repeats that order: the draw is a SplitMix64 stream, so a seed gives one
order on every platform. Classes keep their order, because a class's `#[BeforeClass]` and
`#[AfterClass]` bracket its tests in the report. Report order stays declaration order
([`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict)), so a shuffled run and a plain one print the same report when both
pass. Every test runs in its own isolate ([`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test)), so a random order finds
nothing inside the program. It finds what two tests share outside it, a database or a file, which
[`testing/tests-run-across-every-core`](testing.md#testing-tests-run-across-every-core) leaves to the program to keep apart. `--shuffle` is off by
default.

Under `--format json` and `--format junit` the documents keep their schema, and the not-run count and
the seed are printed on stderr. A `.nvst` tree refuses all three flags: a case is a process of its
own, judged on its whole output, and has no class or seed to shuffle by.

- **Memory:** the failed-test file is one line per failed test, on disk. A shuffled run holds, per
  class, one slot per selected test and the result of each finished test that waits for one written
  above it to start. A run without `--shuffle` holds nothing more.

**Declined:**
- **Shuffling by default.** A run that changes order on its own makes a shared-state failure look like
  a flaky test, and a developer who did not ask for it has no seed in mind to repeat it.
- **The failed-test file in the project folder.** It would appear in every working tree and in
  `git status`, for a fact about one machine's last run.
- **A `--fail-fast` that kills tests already running.** Their result is already being paid for, and a
  killed test would report nothing useful.

<sub>See also [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict), [`testing/tests-run-across-every-core`](testing.md#testing-tests-run-across-every-core), [`testing/tags-and-shards-select-what-runs`](testing.md#testing-tags-and-shards-select-what-runs).</sub>

<a id="testing-watch-reruns-on-an-edit"></a>

## `nvs test --watch` reruns the selection each time a file the program requires changes

`rule:testing/watch-reruns-on-an-edit`

`nvs test --watch` runs the selected tests, then runs them again each time a file the program
requires changes, until it is interrupted.

The change is found by the same background check that brings an edit to a running `nvs run` or
`nvs serve` ([`config/an-edit-reaches-the-next-request-without-a-restart`](config.md#config-an-edit-reaches-the-next-request-without-a-restart)), so `--watch` adds no
second file watcher and sees exactly the files a compile reads. Every pass recompiles what changed and
runs the whole selection: `--filter`, the tag flags and `--rerun-failed` apply to each pass. A pass
that does not compile prints its diagnostics and waits for the next change. A change that arrives while
a pass runs starts the next pass when this one ends, never in the middle of it.

`--watch` runs a program's `#[Test]` methods. It is refused with `--list` and `--update`, which do one
thing and stop, and with a machine format, whose one document per run a consumer reads once. A `.nvst`
tree is not a program and has no require graph to watch, so naming one with `--watch` is refused.

The check is the background check's thread with one more step: it compares the trace of the last
pass's compile (every file read or missed, every `autoload` probe, every listed directory) with the
disk, under the same `[opcache]` `validate`, `revalidate_freq` and `settle`. A folder of programs also
has the folders its files are in listed, so a new file starts a pass. A changed trace is reported once
and disarmed, and the next pass arms the trace of its own compile, which holds what that compile read.
So an edit made while a pass runs is found as soon as that pass ends. The configuration is read once,
when the command starts, and is not watched.

- **Memory:** the background check's one thread, and between passes the trace of the last compile.
  Each pass's program and tests are released when the pass is reported.

**Declined:**
- **Running only the tests a change reaches.** It needs a map from every line to the tests that reach
  it, which only a coverage run builds, and a wrong map skips a test that should have failed.
- **A watcher of its own over the project folder.** It would see files the program never reads, and
  miss none the background check misses.

<sub>See also [`config/an-edit-reaches-the-next-request-without-a-restart`](config.md#config-an-edit-reaches-the-next-request-without-a-restart), [`testing/a-run-can-stop-early-rerun-failures-and-shuffle`](testing.md#testing-a-run-can-stop-early-rerun-failures-and-shuffle).</sub>

<a id="testing-data-rows"></a>

## `#[TestWith]` is matched against the parameters by name and by type, and each row is its own case

`rule:testing/data-rows`

`#[TestWith(...)]` carries an anonymous object that the checker matches against the method's parameters
**by name and by type**. It is the one test marker that may repeat on a declaration, and each row is
its own separately reported case, labelled `method#N` in the order the rows are written — so a row
that fails is reported alone rather than stopping the rows after it, and a skip is stated per row,
a row being a test.

Every way a row and a parameter list fail to line up is one refusal, because the fix is the same
every time: write the row against the parameter list. A field naming no parameter, a value that is
not a literal of that parameter's declared type, a row omitting a field its siblings supply, and the
marker written on a method that is no test at all.

`null` is a literal of a parameter whose type has `null` in it, such as `?int`, and the row fills
that parameter with `null`. At a parameter whose type has no `null`, it is the same refusal.

Where a row and a fixture could both answer one parameter, the **row** wins: it was written against
this method's own parameter list, while a fixture answers every method of the class at once. Each
row's values are folded to constants in parameter order rather than in written order, because that
is the order the call is made in, and are released when that call returns.

<sub>See also [`testing/fixtures`](testing.md#testing-fixtures), [`testing/test-attribute`](testing.md#testing-test-attribute), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats).</sub>

<a id="testing-doubles"></a>

## A double is a shape of callables, structurally checked against an interface

`rule:testing/doubles`

A double is a shape of callables, structurally checked against an interface:
`Core\Test::double<Clock>({now: fn(): Instant => ...})` **is** a `Clock` and may be passed wherever
one is taken. A method the interface does not declare, a method of it the double leaves
unimplemented, and an answer that cannot stand in for the method it names are each a compile error.
The third is [`types/callable-arity`](types.md#types-callable-arity) and [`types/callable-variance`](types.md#types-callable-variance) asked of a callable and
nothing more: a field may declare fewer parameters than the method and accept wider ones, and is
refused only where it would turn away what a call site passes or hand back something that call site
was never promised. `Core\Test::partial<T>($real, {...})` overrides named methods and delegates the
rest to a real implementation.

No class is generated, no source is evaluated, and nothing the author never wrote appears in a
backtrace. There is no builder, no matcher mini-language and no notion of a "nice" or "loose"
double — that last one is not a choice, since a double of `now(): Instant` has nothing legal to
return by default. Every double is strict because nothing else is expressible.

<sub>See also [`testing/interaction-after-the-fact`](testing.md#testing-interaction-after-the-fact), [`testing/assertions-are-typed`](testing.md#testing-assertions-are-typed).</sub>

<a id="testing-interaction-after-the-fact"></a>

## A call to a double is asserted after the exercise, never expected before it

`rule:testing/interaction-after-the-fact`

A double records the calls made to it, and the test asserts on that record afterwards with ordinary
assertions, in the order the test reads: `Core\Test::assertCalled($mailer, Mailer::send, {times: 1,
with: [...]})` and `assertNeverCalled`.

The method named is a compile-checked reference, so renaming it updates or breaks the test and can
never leave one silently passing against a method that no longer exists. It is written bare —
`Mailer::send`, not a callable and not a string — and it is admitted at these argument positions and
nowhere else: everywhere else that spelling reads a class constant and goes on reading one, so no
"method as a value" expression enters the language. What it folds to where it is written is the
method's own name.

There is no `expects()`. An expectation declared before the exercise reads backwards and reports its
failure from a line that is no longer where the problem is.

<sub>See also [`testing/doubles`](testing.md#testing-doubles), [`testing/assertions-are-typed`](testing.md#testing-assertions-are-typed).</sub>

<a id="testing-determinism-declared-on-the-test"></a>

## `at:` and `seed:` fix the clock and the generator of the test's own isolate

`rule:testing/determinism-declared-on-the-test`

`#[Test(at: "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", seed: 42)]` fixes the clock and the random generator of that
test's own isolate: `Core\Time::now()` answers exactly that instant, and the seeded generator and
the identifier members draw the same sequence on every run, every OS and every architecture.
`Core\Test::advance(Duration)` moves the fixed clock forward, and refuses when no clock was fixed —
advancing a real clock is not something a test can ask for. `Core\RateLimit::shed` counts on the
fixed clock too, so `advance` refills an allowance the way waiting would. An `at:` that is not an RFC 3339
timestamp fails that test where it is declared.

Nothing holds state behind a function's back here. The clock is *isolate configuration*, declared at
the test where it is visible and inert everywhere else, in the same category as a time zone set in
`nvs.toml` — and a test declaration reaches no built artifact, so none of this exists in production
even in principle.

**Declined:**
- **A clock parameter as the only way to control time.** It is strictly honest and mirrors the
  seeded generator being a separate type, and it taxes every time-aware class in every program with a
  constructor parameter forever. The attribute is configuration declared at the point of use, and it
  cannot reach production ([`testing/tests-never-reach-a-build`](testing.md#testing-tests-never-reach-a-build)).

<sub>See also [`testing/task-tree-and-virtual-clock`](testing.md#testing-task-tree-and-virtual-clock), [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test), [`testing/tests-never-reach-a-build`](testing.md#testing-tests-never-reach-a-build).</sub>

<a id="testing-task-tree-and-virtual-clock"></a>

## A task still running when a test returns fails that test

`rule:testing/task-tree-and-virtual-clock`

The whole suite runs inside one task, so a test's isolate is a child of it and a `Core\Task::all`
written in a test has a calling task to put its own children under. The runner reads that tree at
the one moment it means anything — when the test's body returns, on the test's own stack — and **a
task still running then fails the test, named as such**. The alternative is what a scheduler does on
its own: cancel the leftovers as the task retires and report a green test that never waited for its
work.

Because the clock is under the test's control, a `Duration` sleep inside a task elapses instantly.
That makes retry, backoff and timeout logic — some of the most error-prone code anyone writes, and
the least tested — testable in microseconds rather than in the seconds it describes.
`Core\Test::assertCompletes(fn, {within: Duration})` states a budget against that same clock.

<sub>See also [`testing/determinism-declared-on-the-test`](testing.md#testing-determinism-declared-on-the-test), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict), [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test).</sub>

<a id="testing-db-transaction"></a>

## `#[Test(db:)]` opens a transaction on the test's own context and rolls it back

`rule:testing/db-transaction`

`#[Test(db: "test")]` opens a transaction against the named connection before the test and rolls it
back after. The test sees a pristine database and writes no cleanup code, and a transaction opened
*inside* the test becomes a savepoint, so code under test that manages its own transaction behaves
normally.

The transaction is opened **on the test's own context, from inside its isolate**, and that is what
makes the savepoint sentence true with no special case anywhere: a connection is memoized on the
context it was opened on, so the test's own `connect("test")` reaches *this* connection and its own
`transaction()` sees a non-zero nesting depth. Opened on the suite's context instead, the two would
contend rather than nest.

The rollback is armed around the whole retry allowance rather than around one attempt, because a
retry calls the method again.

<sub>See also [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test), [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict).</sub>

<a id="testing-in-process-request"></a>

## A test request is dispatched in-process through the compiled route table, and its input arrives `tainted`

`rule:testing/in-process-request`

`Core\Test::request(...)` builds a request and runs it through the compiled route table and the real
middleware chain — no socket, no port, microseconds per test. What answers it is the program's own
entry, run as an isolate with the match already on its carrier, never the matched handler, which
nothing may invoke directly. **An in-process request may not be made from inside one**: the entry
answering it is the entry that asked, so a second would answer itself forever, and the refusal is at
the door rather than at a depth ceiling that would report an engine limit instead of the mistake.

The signature is `Core\Test::request(Core\Http\Method $method, string $path, {headers?:
array<string>, body?: string|bytes, mount?: string, captures?: array<string>}):
Core\Test\Response`. A `?` in `$path` starts the query. A `body` that is not given is no body, which
is not an empty one. `mount` is the prefix the request came in under, `""` for the root, and
`captures` is the list `Core\Request\Mount::captures()` reads back, `{1}` first. The two are one
mount row, so `captures` without a `mount`, or keyed by anything but position, is a `LogicError`:
the root has no pattern to capture.

The response is a `Core`-owned instance whose readings are members, so a status is `status()` and
never a property: `status(): uint`, `body(): string`, `header(string $name): ?string`, `headers():
array<array<string>>`, `cookies(): array<string>`, `json({maxDepth?: uint}): mixed` and
`jsonAs<T>({maxDepth?: uint}): T`. They read a request's answer the way `Core\Request`'s members of
the same names read the request: `header` matches any case and joins repeated lines with `, `,
`headers` keys lower-cased names to lists of lines, and `json`/`jsonAs` carry the same bag, default
and errors. `Set-Cookie` is the one field `header` refuses, as `Core\Http\Response::header` does,
because two cookies joined are neither; `cookies` reads it by name, the last value of a name
winning. The headers are the ones the program's answer carries — its `Content-Type`, or HTML for an
echo, then every header it declared — and not the ones the server adds for itself. A request whose
program fails answers `500`, no body and no headers, which is what the server sends, unless the
program calls `Core\Router::dispatch`: then the answer is what its gate's `failed` wrote, and a request
the door refused is what its gate's `refused` wrote, exactly as the server would send them
([`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler)). Nothing on the
response is `tainted`: it is the program's own output.

The synthetic request's parameters arrive **`tainted`**, exactly as a real request's would, so a
handler that forgets to launder fails its test rather than production.

`#[Test(server: true)]` binds a real listener for the cases that genuinely need the wire. The port
is the operating system's and the address is loopback, so two suites on one machine never collide
and no suite serves the program under test to a network. The listener is a **sibling** of the test's
isolate rather than a child — leftover work is read off the test's own task — and it is retired when
the test that asked for it has joined. It serves under the **default** policy rather than the tree's:
reading a deployment's configuration would make the test's subject the deployment. The two
mechanisms are both kept because they answer measurably different questions: the in-process path
never builds a response head, so the wire is not something it can be asked about.

`Core\Test::serverUrl(): ?string` reads the listener's address back, and is `null` where none was
bound, so it can be called from anywhere. A test reaching its own listener needs the outbound pair
granted — `net.connect` for the host and `net.internal` for loopback
([`http-server/allow-url-pins-the-address`](http-server.md#http-server-allow-url-pins-the-address)) — because nothing about the listener being the
test's own widens that policy.

<sub>See also [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test), [`testing/task-tree-and-virtual-clock`](testing.md#testing-task-tree-and-virtual-clock), [`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler).</sub>

<a id="testing-an-outbound-call-is-answered-from-a-table"></a>

## One registered answer makes every outbound call in that test come from the table, and an unmatched one throws rather than reaching the network

`rule:testing/an-outbound-call-is-answered-from-a-table`

Once a test registers one answer with `Core\Test::answerHttp(string $url, uint $status, {json?, body?,
headers?, tls?})`, **every** outbound call that test makes is answered from the table, and an unmatched
one throws a `LogicError` naming the URL. A `$url` matches exactly, or as a prefix ending in `*`, and
`Core\Test::sentHttp(): array<Core\Test\SentRequest>` hands back what the program sent, in order.

An answer reports no TLS session unless its `tls` option names one:
`Core\Test::tlsSession({version?, cipher?, verified?, subject?, issuer?, expiry?}): Core\Http\TlsInfo`
describes a session over a real leaf certificate for `subject`, signed by a CA certificate for
`issuer`, and every reply that answer serves reports it. A `tls` session on an `http://` URL is a
`LogicError`, because a reply over plain `http` has none.

All-or-nothing is the whole point. A table that answers the calls it knows and lets the rest reach the
network is a suite that passes on a laptop, talks to a partner's production API from CI, and says nothing
about either — so the first registered answer takes the test off the network entirely. A faked call is
still judged where the judging is about *text* — the scheme and the outbound grant, per
[`security/outbound-url-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-outbound-url-is-a-sink) — while resolution and the address check are skipped, there being
no connection for an address to be pinned to
([`http-server/allow-url-pins-the-address`](http-server.md#http-server-allow-url-pins-the-address)). It files no `http` trace event either: nothing crossed a
network.

`SentRequest` is readonly — `method()`, `url()`, `header()` and `body()` — and nothing on it is
`tainted`, unlike every member of a real reply: a sent request is text the program itself authored, which
is the one question [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier) answers. This is what makes the client's own
conformance cases writable with no listener and no outbound grant, the same way
[`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request) makes a request testable with no socket; what it cannot reach is
everything below the table — the pool, the framing, a content coding, a redirect hop, a handshake — which
is proved against a loopback origin instead. A described session is what a handshake *reports*, not a
handshake: nothing verifies its chain and no anchor trusts its CA.

`tlsSession` is what puts the seven `Core\Http\TlsInfo` members within a Novis program's reach without
a network, so each has its example, bench and attack ([`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs)), and a test of a
program that audits its outbound sessions can be written. Every option has a default: `TLSv1.3` over
`TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256` (`TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256` for `TLSv1.2`, the AES-128-GCM
suite each version uses with the leaf's ECDSA key), verified, subject `CN=example.com`, issuer
`CN=Novis Test CA`, and an expiry 90 days after `Core\Time::now()`, so a test with a fixed clock gets
the same value every run. A cipher must be one this build negotiates over that version; a subject or
issuer takes the keys `CN`, `O`, `OU`, `C`, `ST` and `L`, each at most once; an expiry lies between
1950 and the end of 9999. Anything else is a `LogicError` naming the field. The chain is two
certificates, leaf first, each over a fresh P-256 key, because a real server sends its leaf and an
intermediate and a `peerChain()` example should show that order. A prefix row whose URL names no
scheme is not checked for `http://`.

Neither member refuses a call outside a test, for the reason `answerHttp` already gives: nothing
trusts what they build, a reply that reports the session came from the program's own table, which has
already taken it off the network, and no request input reaches the certificate issuer.

- **Memory:** one copy of a described chain, about 1 KB, per registered answer that names a session,
  for the life of the test's context, and a fresh `Core\Http\TlsInfo` per reply that answer serves,
  released with the reply. A program outside a test pays nothing.

**Declined:**
- **Skipping the Novis proofs for `Core\Http\TlsInfo`.** Rust tests alone leave seven public members
  with no example a reader can learn from, and the audit test above still could not be written.
- **A local TLS test server beside `Core\Test::serverUrl`.** A real handshake would need a certificate
  and trust setup and far more code than reading a session back needs. It stays open as a question of
  its own.
- **The session's fields as a nested bag in `answerHttp`'s `tls` option.** An option is never itself a
  bag, so that form would need a compiler change; a member of its own takes an ordinary bag.
- **Seven flat `tls*` options on `answerHttp` in place of the one `tls` option.** They would give
  that member ten options instead of four.
- **A PEM the test pastes in.** It puts a block of base64 in every example, and one certificate
  compiled into the binary could not show three different uses of `subject`.

<sub>See also [`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request), [`testing/doubles`](testing.md#testing-doubles), [`http-server/allow-url-pins-the-address`](http-server.md#http-server-allow-url-pins-the-address).</sub>

<a id="testing-an-outbound-socket-is-answered-by-a-scripted-peer"></a>

## `Core\Test`'s table answers a WebSocket handshake, plays the frames it was given and records what the program sent, and an unmatched socket throws rather than connecting

`rule:testing/an-outbound-socket-is-answered-by-a-scripted-peer`

A test answers an outbound socket from `Core\Test`'s table, never from a listener. `Core\Test::answerSocket`
registers a URL with the frames a peer should send, beside the `answerHttp` that
[`testing/an-outbound-call-is-answered-from-a-table`](testing.md#testing-an-outbound-call-is-answered-from-a-table) gives an outbound call; a socket matching that URL
completes its handshake **without connecting**, receives those frames in order and then a close, and
`Core\Test::sentSocket` reads back every frame the program sent. A socket the table does not match throws
naming the URL, exactly as an unmatched call does, so a test that forgot to script a peer fails saying so
rather than reaching the network.

This is what makes a conformance case over a WebSocket writable at all: no port, no listener, no timing
assumption, and the same determinism every other test in the suite has
([`testing/determinism-declared-on-the-test`](testing.md#testing-determinism-declared-on-the-test)). A scripted socket is still refused for anything the real
one would be refused for — a `tainted` URL, a scheme the row does not serve, a host outside the grant —
because the table answers a call that has already passed every question
([`http-server/an-outbound-socket-is-opened-like-an-outbound-call`](http-server.md#http-server-an-outbound-socket-is-opened-like-an-outbound-call)), and a received payload is
`tainted` there as it is on the wire.

What a scripted peer cannot reach is proved against a loopback peer in Rust, not approximated here:
masking, fragmentation, the close handshake and a ping are `tungstenite`'s behaviour rather than Novis's
surface, and a table that pretended to them would be asserting its own implementation.

<sub>See also [`testing/an-outbound-call-is-answered-from-a-table`](testing.md#testing-an-outbound-call-is-answered-from-a-table), [`testing/determinism-declared-on-the-test`](testing.md#testing-determinism-declared-on-the-test), [`http-server/an-outbound-socket-is-opened-like-an-outbound-call`](http-server.md#http-server-an-outbound-socket-is-opened-like-an-outbound-call).</sub>

<a id="testing-property-testing"></a>

## `#[Property]` derives its generators from the parameters' declared types

`rule:testing/property-testing`

`#[Property]` runs a method against generated inputs, and the generators are **derived from the
parameters' declared types** by the same declaration walk a codec is derived from, user classes
included. That is why this belongs to the compiler rather than to a package: only a compiler can
walk a declared type, and a userland version needs a hand-written generator per type, which is the
boilerplate that keeps property testing rare.

A failure shrinks to a minimal counterexample and reports the seed that reproduces it exactly. A
`gen:` option narrows one parameter where its declared type is wider than the domain. A generated
`string` is valid UTF-8 including combining marks and grapheme clusters, because that is what a
`string` is — a property that only holds for ASCII is a property that is not true.

**The attribute.** `#[Core\Test\Property]` goes on a method with a `#[Test]`'s shape: `public`, not
`static`, `: void`, with a body. Its options are `#[Test]`'s less `retries:` and `because:`, plus
`runs:` (1 to 100000, 100 by default) and `gen:`. It is test code
([`testing/tests-never-reach-a-build`](testing.md#testing-tests-never-reach-a-build)). **Every parameter is generated**: a `#[TestWith]` row, a
second marker, and a fixture are never asked. Its rows ride in their own table, beside the `#[Test]`
one (`crates/nvs-types/src/property.rs`).

**What has a generator.** Every scalar, `decimal`, `bytes`, a `string` and either `tainted` form, an
enum and a single case, a single-value type, `mixed`, `?T`, `array<T>`, an inline shape, a union, and a
concrete, non-generic class of the program with a `public` constructor, built from its constructor's
parameters. A class may reach itself through `?T`, a list or a union. Anything else is `E0890` at the
method: a function, an interface, an abstract or `Core` class, a class that contains itself with
nothing between, and a `secret` value, because a failing input is printed.

**`gen:`** is `{<parameter>: "<low>..<high>"}`, both ends inclusive. A number's range bounds the
value; a `string`'s, `bytes`' or `array<T>`'s bounds the length, in grapheme clusters for a string, up
to 10000. A `?T` parameter narrows its `T`. An entry naming no parameter, a range that does not parse,
and a range on a type with no range are `E0890`.

**The values.** A SplitMix64 stream seeded from the run's seed and the call's index, and nothing
else, so one seed gives one sequence of inputs. Call `i` of `n` has a size rising from 0 to 100, which
caps every length's share of its range, and a number takes one of its range's edges about one call in
eight. A float is finite. A string's pieces are ASCII, control characters, code points of two, three
and four bytes, and clusters of several code points: combining marks, U+200D emoji sequences, flags,
Hangul jamo and a Devanagari conjunct (`crates/nvs-types/src/property/generate.rs`).

**The run.** `nvs test` reports each `#[Property]` as one test, and calls it `runs:` times, each on a
fresh instance in the test's own isolate. The seed is `seed:`, or a random one, and it also seeds the
isolate's own random numbers. The first call that fails ends the run. A subclass runs every property
it inherits, under its own name, as it does a `#[Test]` ([`testing/hook-inheritance`](testing.md#testing-hook-inheritance)).

**The shrink.** A failing call's inputs shrink in the same isolate, one parameter at a time and
simplest first, through candidates their own generator could have made, so a shrunk input still fits
its declared type and its `gen:` range (`crates/nvs-types/src/property/shrink.rs`). Each candidate is
one call on a fresh instance, at most 1000 of them. Only the last failing call's assertions are
reported, beside one more failure naming the call, the shrunk inputs, the generated inputs and the
`#[Property(seed: n)]` that runs them again. The JSON report carries the same as the test's
`counterexample` ([`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats)). A candidate that does not build, or that calls
`exit()`, is not a failure, and the shrink stops at the test's wall-time limit
([`testing/a-test-has-a-wall-time-limit`](testing.md#testing-a-test-has-a-wall-time-limit)) with the last real failure. Nothing in it is random, so
one seed shrinks to one counterexample on every platform.

- **Memory:** one call's inputs hold at most 2^20 elements, bytes and string pieces together, per
  property in flight. An input whose shortest form is over that is refused before it is built. A
  failure also keeps its generated inputs while it shrinks, and one candidate at a time: a candidate
  is built when it is tried, so a step costs what it tries and never the square of an input's
  length.

**Declined:**
- **`retries:` on a property.** A failure is reproduced from its seed and shrunk, so a retry would
  only hide the input that broke it.
- **A fixture filling a property's parameter.** A parameter is generated or it is not, and a fixture's
  value cannot be shrunk.
- **NaN and the infinities by default.** Most numeric code is not written for them, so every property
  over a `float` would first have to exclude them.
- **A `gen:` that names a generator function.** A range is checked when the program compiles and says
  the domain where it is written; a function is a second place to read.
- **A shrink that calls a test hook less, or runs candidates on other cores.** Each candidate is a call
  of the test, so it runs exactly as the failing call did, `#[AfterEachTest]` included, and the
  greedy walk needs each answer before it picks the next candidate.

<sub>See also [`testing/data-rows`](testing.md#testing-data-rows), [`testing/assertions-are-typed`](testing.md#testing-assertions-are-typed).</sub>

<a id="testing-inline-snapshots"></a>

## A snapshot is a literal in the test body, and the updater rewrites that literal and nothing else

`rule:testing/inline-snapshots`

`Core\Test::assertMatchesInline($value, "...")` holds the expectation in the source file, and
`nvs test --update` splices the produced value into that literal. Inline rather than a separate
snapshot file, because the failure mode of snapshot testing is a reviewer approving a diff they did
not read, and a diff inside the test body is one they will.

The updater is the one thing in `nvs test` that writes to a source file, and what it writes is the
expected literal and nothing else. The literal's span comes from a compile-time row per **written**
call, joined to the run by the test the mismatch happened in — the method is load-bearing, because
this workflow starts every snapshot empty and two of them would otherwise share one key. Where that
join is not a single site, nothing is written and the run names it: a rendering placed under a
snapshot nobody asserted is worse than the failing test it replaced.

What is written is a single-quoted literal, so a multi-line rendering stays multi-line and reads as
a diff. A run that rewrote a snapshot still reports the test as failed; the re-run is what says the
new text is the one the author meant. The rendering is canonical, ordered, and redacts a `secret`,
so a snapshot cannot become the place secrets get committed.

**Declined:**
- **Separate snapshot files.** They are better for very large payloads, and worse at the thing that
  actually goes wrong: a reviewer approving a snapshot diff unread.
- **Snapshots in a library.** The updater needs the written literal's span, which only the compiler
  records, so a library version would be permanently worse rather than merely external.

<sub>See also [`testing/assertions-are-typed`](testing.md#testing-assertions-are-typed), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats).</sub>

<a id="testing-mutation-testing"></a>

## A mutation run asks whether any test would have noticed the code being wrong

`rule:testing/mutation-testing`

A mutation run makes a small, deliberate change to the code, re-runs the tests, and records whether
anything failed. It is the measurement that closes the gap coverage leaves: a line having run says
nothing about whether an assertion would have objected had it been wrong, and a suite at full line
coverage routinely misses most introduced defects.

Two things make the built-in version categorically better than an external one, and neither is
available outside the compiler. Mutants are generated from typed IR, so every one is type-valid and
compiles, where a tool mutating a syntax tree pays a compile to discover that many do not. And
mutant runs are **coverage-directed**: the probe data says which tests touch the mutated line, so a
mutant runs against those rather than against the whole suite. On two thousand tests and five
hundred mutants that is the difference between minutes and most of a day.

**A mutant is one changed site in the lowered program.** Parse and check run once; lowering takes the
checked tree and a mutant key, makes exactly one change at the site the key names, and codegen
compiles the whole program from that. A key is the site's file, line and change, so a report names a
mutant the way a reader finds it. No mutant is made from test code
([`testing/tests-never-reach-a-build`](testing.md#testing-tests-never-reach-a-build)'s marker methods, and every body written inside one), so a
mutant changes the program under test and never the test that judges it.

The first operator set is six swaps, each keeping its operands' and its result's types, so every
mutant lowers and compiles with no second check:

| Operator | Change |
|---|---|
| relational boundary | `<` ↔ `<=`, `>` ↔ `>=` |
| equality negated | `==` ↔ `!=` |
| arithmetic swap | `+` ↔ `-`, `*` ↔ `/` |
| logical connector | `&&` ↔ `\|\|` |
| boolean literal | `true` ↔ `false` |
| branch condition negated | an `if`'s or a loop's condition is inverted |

A swap is made only where it keeps the result type, so `*` and `/` swap over `float` and `decimal`
alone. A condition the checker narrows a type on (an `is` test, or an `==` against a literal, `null`
or a class constant) keeps its direction, its connectors and that test. A `true` or `false` that is a
condition, a `match` subject or an `==` operand keeps its value. A mutant that took a narrowed edge
with the test false would read a value at a type it does not have.

The set is enumerated where it is implemented, so adding an operator changes no rule.

`--mutate` runs on a program's `#[Test]` methods only. On a `.nvst` tree it exits with an error, as
the coverage flags do, because per-test coverage exists only for program tests.

**The run.** `nvs test --mutate` runs the selected tests once with coverage, as a coverage flag does
([`testing/coverage-report`](testing.md#testing-coverage-report)), and reports that run as any run is reported. A test that fails there
fails the run, and no mutant runs: a mutant is judged against a suite that passes without it. Then
each mutant runs the selected tests that reached the statement it changes, the innermost statement
whose span holds the changed expression, up to `--jobs` at once, and no further test starts once one
has failed. A test with no wall-time limit gets one for a mutant run, ten times the slowest test of
the coverage run plus one second, because a mutant can make a loop that never ends; a test with its
own limit keeps it ([`testing/a-test-has-a-wall-time-limit`](testing.md#testing-a-test-has-a-wall-time-limit)).

Each mutant has one of four outcomes:

| Outcome | When |
|---|---|
| `killed` | a test failed or called `exit` |
| `timed out` | no test failed, and a test ran past its wall-time limit |
| `survived` | every test it ran passed, a flaky one included |
| `not reached` | no selected test reached its statement, so nothing ran |

The score is killed plus timed out over every mutant but the unreached ones. The human report prints
the four counts and the score after the run's summary, then each survived mutant with its file, line
and change. `--format json` writes `schemaVersion: 4` ([`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats)): version 3's
document, plus a `mutants` array with one record per mutant, `{file, line, change, outcome, tests}`,
in the order the program lowers its sites. `tests` is how many tests reached the mutant's line, which
is what the covering-test filter decides and what the bench of a mutation run counts. A JUnit document has no place for a mutant, so `--mutate` with
`--format junit` exits with an error. The exit status is the coverage run's: a survived mutant does not
fail the run.

**What it costs:** nothing for a run without `--mutate`, and nothing on the request path. A mutation
run pays one coverage run, then one lowering and codegen of the whole program per mutant, plus the
tests that reach the mutant's line. A mutant compiles with no artifact cache, since its key would be
the unchanged program's. Memory is O(`--jobs`): one mutant runs at a time, with its tests in flight,
and the run keeps one record per mutant for the report.

Since the mutants grow with the program and each compiles all of it, a run's compile time grows with
the square of the program's size; that is the price of the whole-program recompile, and a team runs
`--mutate` on a schedule, such as a nightly CI job, not on every save. What the covering-test
filter decides is measured: `benches/scaling/testing/mutate.nvs` grows the suite around a fixed
program under test, and its ramp fails when the test runs per mutant grow with the suite.

**Declined:**

- *Mutating the syntax tree.* Each mutant would pay a check to find out whether it compiles, and the
  tree has no types for a swap to keep.
- *Recompiling only the mutated function.* It needs a partial-recompile mechanism kept correct beside
  the whole-program one, for a cost the per-mutant test run already outweighs.
- *Running several mutants at once.* Each would hold a compiled unit and its tests' isolates, and
  `--jobs` already fills the cores with one mutant's tests.
- *A per-test limit from each test's own coverage-run time.* It is closer for a fast test, and it
  needs a table carried into every test's run; one bound for the run is one number.

<sub>See also [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`testing/isolate-per-test`](testing.md#testing-isolate-per-test), [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs).</sub>

<a id="testing-runner-is-strict"></a>

## A test that asserts nothing fails, a skip states a reason, and a retry is reported flaky rather than green

`rule:testing/runner-is-strict`

A test that asserts nothing fails — the ledger already knows the count, and
`Core\Test::assertDoesNotThrow(callable)` is how a test states "this must merely not throw",
explicitly.

A skip states a reason: `skip: true` is a compile error and a written sentence is not, and an empty
or blank one is `E0880`. A retry states one too — `retries:` with no `because:` beside it is refused
