where it is written, a blank `because:` is `E0880`, and so is a `retries:` below 1 — and a test
that passed on a later attempt is its own verdict, `flaky`, never green: its own mark, its own count
in every summary, and the element CI systems already read as "passed, but it flaked". It carries the
**last failed** attempt's message, the attempt that passed having produced nothing to report. Only a
failure is retried: a skip never ran, and an `exit(n)` ended the program rather than the test. A
flaky test does not fail the run — what this takes away is the silence, not the green build.

Report order is **declaration order**, even though execution is unordered, because stable output is
worth a great deal. Total isolation makes execution order irrelevant inside the program. What a random
start order can still find is state two tests share outside it, and
[`testing/a-run-can-stop-early-rerun-failures-and-shuffle`](testing.md#testing-a-run-can-stop-early-rerun-failures-and-shuffle) shuffles the start order without
changing the report's.

<sub>See also [`testing/failure-ledger`](testing.md#testing-failure-ledger), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats), [`testing/task-tree-and-virtual-clock`](testing.md#testing-task-tree-and-virtual-clock), [`testing/db-transaction`](testing.md#testing-db-transaction).</sub>

<a id="testing-report-formats"></a>

## One verdict, three renderings, a machine format owns stdout alone, and the JSON one locates every test it reports

`rule:testing/report-formats`

Human output is the default and is written as the run goes, which is what keeps a long suite
legible. A JUnit XML document and a versioned JSON one are each written whole at the end, because
neither has a prefix worth streaming. JUnit XML rather than a Novis-native document, because it is
what every CI system already ingests. All three render the same case list and a verdict is decided
**once**, so the plaintext mark, the JSON string and the XML element cannot disagree about how a
test came out.

Under a machine format the program's own output goes to **stderr**, a failed test's always and a
passing test's under `--show-output`: the redirect that produces the
document makes stdout the document, and a test's `echo` interleaved into it would produce something
no parser accepts. It is not quoted back into the document either — a whole suite's output is a cost
every run would pay for the few being debugged. A machine format also names a `#[Test]` run, so
asking for one over a `.nvst` tree is refused rather than silently ignored: the two share no summary,
so there is no document for it to be about.

The JSON schema is versioned and carries what XML has nowhere to put: a structured diff, per-row
results, a shrunk counterexample and per-test coverage. It is at `schemaVersion: 2`, where every record
says where its test is written — `file`, `line` and `column`, one-based, the same location
`nvs check --json` carries for a diagnostic — because a `class` and a `method` are enough to print a
line and not enough to open a file, and nothing below the compiler can recover the rest. The JUnit and
plaintext renderings are unchanged: JUnit has no version to raise, and a path on every line is noise for
the reader the plaintext one is written for. Under a coverage flag ([`testing/coverage-report`](testing.md#testing-coverage-report)) the
document is `schemaVersion: 3`, and every record also carries `coverage`: each file name mapped to the
sorted lines that test reached in any attempt. A run without one writes version 2 unchanged. Under
`--mutate` ([`testing/mutation-testing`](testing.md#testing-mutation-testing)) it is `schemaVersion: 4`: version 3's document plus a
`mutants` array, one `{file, line, change, outcome, tests}` record per mutant. A failed
`#[Property]` also carries `counterexample` ([`testing/property-testing`](testing.md#testing-property-testing)): `{seed, call, inputs,
generatedInputs}`, each input as the report prints it and `inputs` shrunk. It is a new key and needs
no new version, because a consumer that does not read it reads the rest unchanged.

**`--list` is the same run's table, without the run.** It answers from the `#[Test]` table the compile
already built, so a program whose tests fail, hang or `exit` lists exactly as a passing one does, and its
document carries one `{class, method, file, line, column}` per call under `listed` — no verdict and no
summary, since a summary of zeros is a report of a run that did not happen and a `tests` array missing
its verdicts would make a consumer tell the two documents apart by a key's absence. `--format junit`,
`--update` and `--record` are each refused beside it rather than ignored.

**`--list` over a `.nvst` tree lists its cases**, in the same document: one `{case, file, line, column}`
per case, where `case` and `file` are the path a run's report names the case by and the location is
line 1. `case` takes the place of `class` and `method`, because a case is a file, and it is the key a
consumer tells the two kinds of record apart by. The selection is the run's own: `--filter`,
`--shard` and `--cases` apply, and no case is read. Under `--list`, a directory with any `.nvst`
file under it is a case tree even when it also holds programs, so an editor lists a workspace's cases
by naming the workspace folder. A run of such a directory is still refused, because it would report
two suites in one call ([`testing/nvst-is-separate`](testing.md#testing-nvst-is-separate)). Both directory walks, the case tree's and a
directory program's, skip a linked directory and a directory that a `CACHEDIR.TAG` marks as a cache,
and walk with a stack of their own, so no tree's depth can overflow the thread's stack.

- **Memory:** the compiler holds one span per `#[Test]` row for the life of a compile, on a table that
  exists only for a program that declares tests. A run holds one resolved path, line and column per
  reported case.

**Declined:**
- **A second document for discovery, with its own version.** It is two schemas to freeze and two
  consumers to write, and a location spelled twice. The version number exists so one document can
  grow.

<sub>See also [`testing/runner-is-strict`](testing.md#testing-runner-is-strict), [`testing/data-rows`](testing.md#testing-data-rows), [`testing/nvst-is-separate`](testing.md#testing-nvst-is-separate), [`ide/the-test-tree-is-discovered-and-run-through-the-cli`](ide.md#ide-the-test-tree-is-discovered-and-run-through-the-cli).</sub>

<a id="testing-coverage-report"></a>

## `nvs test` writes line, function and branch coverage as lcov, Clover and Cobertura, from one hit table every context of the run counts into

`rule:testing/coverage-report`

`nvs test --coverage-lcov <FILE>`, `--coverage-clover <FILE>` and `--coverage-cobertura <FILE>` write
which lines and branches a program's `#[Test]` run reached, and a run may write any of them together.
Every line a statement starts on is listed with the largest count of the statements starting on it;
every function is compiled, so a line no test reached reads `0`. lcov and Clover also list every
`nvs_ir::Function` that has a statement, under the IR's name, at the line of its first statement and
with that statement's count. Every format lists every `Terminator::Branch` at the line its condition
starts on, with how often its true and its false side ran: lcov as `BRDA` lines with `BRF`/`BRH`, and
`-` for both sides of a branch that never ran; Clover as a `<line type="cond">` with `truecount` and
`falsecount` and two `conditionals` per branch; Cobertura as `branch="true"` and a
`condition-coverage` on the line and a `branch-rate`. A `Terminator::Switch` has no probe and is in no
report. Cobertura groups the files into one package per directory and gives a `line-rate` and a
`branch-rate` at every level. A file not on disk is left out, and a file is named relative to the
directory the run started in, with `/` between parts. The flags are refused beside a `.nvst` tree and
beside `--list`, and under a machine `--format` stdout is still that format's document alone.

The counts come from [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes)'s statement and edge probes. Codegen adds a
per-function base to each `StmtId` and each `EdgeId`, so the number a probe passes names one statement
or one edge in the whole program, and `nvs_ir::Program::stmt_spans` and `edge_spans` are the tables of
where each is written. Every coverage flag turns both `DebugFlags::COVERAGE` and `DebugFlags::BRANCH`
on and gives the suite's context one `StmtHits` table with a counter per statement and per edge; every
context the run makes from it — each test's isolate, a fixture, an in-process request, a request a
`server: true` test sends — counts into that one table. Novis code cannot read it. A run that does not
ask makes no table.

The IR keeps its ids per function, so an edit in one function does not renumber every other one, and
only codegen and the report need a program-wide number. A unit loaded from the compile cache was
compiled by the same walk, so the runner computes the tables from the lowered program without the
compile. One table handed down with the flag word reaches every context the same way the flag does,
including a request a `server: true` test sends, which runs in a context no test owns, and a placed
isolate, which ends on another core. A connection the server accepts starts from a fresh context, so
the runner's request program installs the table and the flag on it itself. A context with the flag and
no table counts nothing. A line takes the largest count of its statements, not their sum, so a `while`
and the block it opens are not counted twice. A file's own top-level statements do not run under
`nvs test`, so they read `0`.

One table feeds all three formats, so the files cannot disagree about a count. Cobertura is the
format GitLab and Azure DevOps read, branches are what a reviewer asks for, and a function record is
what most coverage dashboards summarise first. A function's count is its first statement's, which
runs exactly when the function does; a function with no statement has no probe and is not listed,
the same rule a line follows. Every coverage flag turns both bits on, and no flag counts lines
without branches. The suite runs one test at a time, so the lines each test reached
([`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats)) are the statements whose count in the shared table grew while it ran.
The VS Code extension's Coverage run profile runs the same command with `--coverage-lcov` into its
storage directory and reads that file into the editor's own coverage view, drawing nothing of its own
([`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has)).

**Memory:** per run that asks, one `u64` per statement and per edge in the program, and one file and
line pair per statement for the report. A run that does not ask spends nothing. With coverage on, each
statement executed costs one relaxed atomic add beside the call the probe already made. Per-test lines
cost one copy of the statement table per test while a JSON document is being written.

**Declined:**
- **Program-wide statement numbers in the IR.** An edit in one function would renumber every other
  one, and nothing outside a coverage run needs a program-wide number.
- **Copying each isolate's counts back to its parent when it ends.** A request a `server: true` test
  sends runs in a context no test owns, and a placed isolate ends on another core, so each path would
  need its own copy step.
- **A probe of its own at each function's entry.** The first statement's probe already counts it, and
  a second site would cost every call a load and a branch for a number the table already has.
- **Branch counts derived from the statement counts**, as a condition's count minus the first
  statement of each side. A side with no statement of its own, such as an `if` with no `else`, has
  nothing to subtract, and the result would be a guess.
- **A table per test.** While the runner runs one test at a time, the shared table's counts before and
  after a test name exactly its lines. A runner that runs tests in parallel gives each test a table of
  its own.

<sub>See also [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats).</sub>

<a id="testing-nvst-is-separate"></a>

## `.nvst` proves the language; `#[Test]` is how a program written in Novis tests itself

`rule:testing/nvst-is-separate`

`.nvst` is a whole-program, expected-stdout conformance case, and it is how **Novis's own conformance
to its specification** is proven. A case's expectation is what the rules say Novis prints. No test
and no check runs another language's engine to judge Novis, for this repository or for a user: the
rules and the conformance cases are the one reference.

`#[Test]` is how **a program written in Novis** tests itself.

The two formats answer different questions and are not unified, now or later. `nvs test` runs
both — a path of `.nvst` files, or a program's compiled test table — and reports each in the shape
that fits it.

**Declined:**
- **A PHP oracle**: an `--ORACLE--` section run under PHP, an `nvs test --php` mode, or a differential
  tree kept as an unrun archive. It is a second reference that disagrees with the rules wherever they
  diverge, and a reader cannot tell which one is normative.

<sub>See also [`testing/test-attribute`](testing.md#testing-test-attribute), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats), [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-directory-of-programs-is-one-test-program"></a>

## A directory handed to `nvs test` that holds `.nvs` files is one program requiring every one of them in name order, and a file in it that requires the bootstrap gives it its `autoload` map

`rule:testing/a-directory-of-programs-is-one-test-program`

A directory handed to `nvs test` that holds `.nvs` files is one program: the runner writes an entry
that requires every `.nvs` file under the directory that no other file under it requires,
subdirectories walked, in name order, and runs that program's test table. The entry is never put on
disk, and its one job is to bring every file into the compile.

The directory carries its own `autoload` map. Declarations reach the program the way they reach any
program, through a file the entry requires. Run over a project's root — `nvs test .`, the command
the website teaches — that file is the project's own entry file, so tests written under the autoload
root, beside the classes they test or in a class of their own, need nothing else, and the editor
lends them the same map because the root owns them. A directory of tests outside every autoload root
— a project's `tests/` — holds one file that requires the application's bootstrap, and every other
file in it requires nothing; the editor needs that file to lend the map, and the project's root still
runs as one program with both. A directory holding no such file compiles as it is, which is right
for tests that need no class outside themselves and reports `E0306` for the rest, exactly as running
the same files by hand would.

- **A file another file requires is reached through it.** `require` has no once-only guard
  ([`statements/require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct`](statements.md#statements-require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct)) and `Core\Test::request` runs the
  program, requires included, so an entry that required the project's entry beside a bootstrap that
  requires it would run it twice per request. The edges are the ones the name-resolution walk
  resolves, so the runner agrees with the build on what a path names, and a directory whose files
  hold no `require` walks nothing first.
- **One program per call.** A second path beside a program is refused with a sentence about the
  count: `nvs test .` over the root is how a project with tests in two places runs them together.
- **Name order, not test order.** The order the files are required in decides nothing a reader can
  see: classes are reported in name order and methods in declaration order, whatever brought them in.
- **A file is a program, a directory of files is a program, and a directory holding both `.nvs` and
  `.nvst` files is refused**, since the two suites share no report
  ([`testing/nvst-is-separate`](testing.md#testing-nvst-is-separate)). A directory holding only `.nvst` files is the case tree it always
  was.
- **The configuration is folded for the directory.** An `[[app]]` block whose `root` contains it
  applies; an `entry` glob names a file and matches no directory.
- **The editor reads the directory the same way.** A plain file under the directory of a file that
  requires the bootstrap is analysed through that bootstrap's map
  ([`ide/an-autoloaded-file-borrows-its-programs-map`](ide.md#ide-an-autoloaded-file-borrows-its-programs-map)).

A new test file is in the suite the moment it exists, and nothing is added to the language, the
configuration or the command line for it. The cost is one directory walk per invocation before the
compile, and a compile that requires as many files as a hand-written entry naming each one would.
Nothing is on a request path of the runtime.

**Memory:** the written entry is one string, held for the run.

**Declined:**
- **A glob in a literal `require`**, `require 'tests/*Test.nvs';`. A `require` site is one call to
  one file's script frame, and a site that expands to many files reaches into the type checker and
  the compiler for a feature the tests never execute.
- **A `[test]` block naming a bootstrap and directories.** The configuration is per server and an
  application's tests are per application, the editor reads no `--config`, and a suite would need a
  setting before its first run.
- **A `--bootstrap` flag beside the directory.** Every run would spell it, and the editor cannot
  see it.
- **Running each `.nvs` file under the directory as its own program.** A test file that requires
  nothing resolves nothing, and a report per file has no summary.
- **Requiring the bootstrap from every test file.** It is one line per file across the suite, the
  same list an entry naming every file is.
- **Reading the directory as a program only when it holds no `index.nvs`.** It is a convention on a
  name the runner would have to explain, for a case the mixed-directory refusal already covers.

<sub>See also [`testing/nvst-is-separate`](testing.md#testing-nvst-is-separate), [`programs/autoload`](programs.md#programs-autoload), [`ide/an-autoloaded-file-borrows-its-programs-map`](ide.md#ide-an-autoloaded-file-borrows-its-programs-map).</sub>

<a id="testing-one-slice-is-one-feature"></a>

## One slice writes all of a feature's proofs together

`rule:testing/one-slice-is-one-feature`

One slice takes one feature and writes **all of its feature proofs together**. The expensive thing a
session buys is understanding what the feature does at its edges, and the description, the test, the
examples, the bench and the attack all spend that same understanding; split across one session per
proof it is bought once per proof, against a fixed per-session cost that does not shrink with the size
of the work.

The generated work chain is one goal per group of features sharing an implementing file set, each
carrying a context manifest naming that file set and each gated by a command that exits non-zero.
Regenerating the chain is how it stays current: a group that owes nothing is left out, so a second
emission writes the chain that is *left*.

**Declined:**
- **One proof per session.** It buys the same understanding of the feature once per proof.

<sub>See also [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs), [`testing/a-failing-proof-is-fixed-or-recorded`](testing.md#testing-a-failing-proof-is-fixed-or-recorded), [`testing/roster-is-derived`](testing.md#testing-roster-is-derived).</sub>

<a id="testing-examples-live-in-the-repository"></a>

## `docs/examples/` is the only copy of every example, and the website reads it in place

`rule:testing/examples-live-in-the-repository`

`docs/examples/` is the only copy of every example, and the website build reads it in place. Nothing
copies it into `website/`, so there is no mirror to rebuild and no second copy to fall out of date.

They live in the repository because the same sweep that tests a feature writes its examples, and a
sweep cannot write into a tree it is not allowed to touch.

**Declined:**
- **Examples in the website's own tree, written by a person after the feature ships.** Written that
  way, almost no member ever had one. The sweep that understands the feature is the one that writes
  them.
- **A mirror of the examples under `website/`, kept equal by a sync script and a check.** Two copies of
  every example, and a failure mode, the mirror being behind, whose only fix is to run the script that
  should have run.

<sub>See also [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs), [`testing/proof-attribution`](testing.md#testing-proof-attribution), [`testing/website-pages-are-stamped`](testing.md#testing-website-pages-are-stamped).</sub>

<a id="testing-website-pages-are-stamped"></a>

## A website page lists the features it covers, and the session that changes one rereads and re-stamps its pages

`rule:testing/website-pages-are-stamped`

Every handwritten website page lists in `covers:` the proofs roster's ids of the features it explains,
and `website/site.lock.json` records the hash each feature had when the page was last reread against
it. The hash covers the feature's help card or reference section, its `about.md` and its examples.

A covered id the roster no longer has is **broken**. A covered feature whose hash moved since the
page's stamp is **stale**. `bun nv site --check` refuses every broken id and every stale page, and
CI's `proofs` job runs it over the whole tree. The session that changes a feature rereads the pages
that cover it, fixes them and runs `bun nv site --stamp`, the same way it owes the feature's proofs. A
stamp is written by whoever reread the page, never to quiet the check.

The generated half of the site, the reference, is rewritten from the binary and the roster on every
render and cannot drift; the handwritten half can, because nothing else connects a guide to the
behaviour it explains. A hash makes exactly the pages that cover a changed feature stale, and the
session that changed it is the one holding the context to reread them. `covers:` uses the roster's
ids, so a page and a feature proof name a feature the same way. The cost is that a change to a
feature costs its author a reread of the pages that cover it. `bun nv site` is one tool that holds the
guard, the stamp, the build and every `--check` part, in place of a script per check, and its parts
run in the CI job that has already built `nvs`, because the snippets and the roster both need it.

**A page's search questions are stamped as the page is.** Each entry of `website/src/data/questions.json`
records the feature its questions were written from and that feature's hash, and an entry whose hash
moved is stale. `bun nv site --check questions` fails on every stale or broken entry and on every
built page with no entry, so a new page fails CI until it has questions. It also holds each entry to
four to six questions of at most 15 words, in the words of § *Text an end user reads*, with no question
two pages share. `bun nv site --questions --stamp` is run by whoever rewrote or reread them. The
questions are not a feature proof.

Every snippet a page shows lives under `website/snippets/`, and that same CI step checks each file
beside it against the real binary. A `.err` is the diagnostic `nvs check` must report for a program that
does not compile. A `.out` is what `nvs run` must print with exit 0. A `.http.out` is the response body
a real `nvs serve` sends for the request the snippet's `.nvsr` describes, or for a plain `GET` when it
has none; no simulated request stands in for a server. A snippet with a `.nvsr` always has a `.http.out`.
A `.tainted` lists each token `nvs lsp` gives the `tainted` modifier, which the page shows with a dotted
underline and a tooltip, and a snippet with no such token has none: the grammar that colours the code
cannot know which values are tainted, and the server that knows is the one an editor asks.

**Where the command line and a server print different things, the page shows both**, the command line
first. `echo` writes to a different sink in each ([`tooling/echo-always-has-a-sink`](tooling.md#tooling-echo-always-has-a-sink)), and in a
response it escapes markup characters ([`core-classes/html-auto-escape`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-auto-escape)), so a program that echoes
`<`, `&` or a quote prints one text and sends another. The check runs every snippet that compiles in
both contexts, and where both apply and differ it requires both files; where they agree it requires
one and refuses the second. **The front page shows only what the server sends**, with `<Snippet
output="http">`, because a web server is what a visitor first comes to Novis for. So no page carries
Novis code that is not known to run, and no output a page shows differs from what the binary prints in
the context the page names.

**Declined:**
- **Staleness by a "last reviewed" date.** A date says nothing about whether the feature moved since.
- **A periodic review pass.** It finds drift late, and never says which page a change reached.

<sub>See also [`testing/examples-live-in-the-repository`](testing.md#testing-examples-live-in-the-repository), [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs), [`tooling/echo-always-has-a-sink`](tooling.md#tooling-echo-always-has-a-sink), [`core-classes/html-auto-escape`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-auto-escape).</sub>

<a id="testing-the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool"></a>

## The website's Tools area has an overview and one page for each developer tool, every page about running a tool lives there, and a page that moved there leaves nothing behind  *(designed — owned by goal tools-website)*

`rule:testing/the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool`

The website has a Tools area, the fourth after Guides, Syntax and Reference and before In-Depth, with
an overview page and one page for each developer tool: the debug viewer, the debugger, the profiler,
the editor, the formatter, the test runner, the API document and the CLI. The overview shows each tool
with one picture and one line and links to its page. Each tool is a directory under `tools/`, its page
the directory's `index.mdx`, and a tool with more than one page keeps the rest beside it, as the test
runner keeps coverage.

Every picture on these pages is generated from a real run and checked, never drawn by hand: a terminal
block ([`testing/a-terminal-block-shows-what-nvs-printed`](testing.md#testing-a-terminal-block-shows-what-nvs-printed)), an editor replay
([`testing/a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned`](testing.md#testing-a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned)), a debugger replay
([`testing/a-debugger-replay-plays-what-nvs-dap-returned`](testing.md#testing-a-debugger-replay-plays-what-nvs-dap-returned)) or a screenshot
([`testing/a-screenshot-is-taken-from-a-real-run`](testing.md#testing-a-screenshot-is-taken-from-a-real-run)). A picture nothing checks shows a tool as it
was, and nothing notices when it changes.

**A page's place is its subject.** A page about using one of these tools lives under Tools. A page
about writing Novis code, or about running a program in production, stays where it is: a guide to
testing a route writes code, and a guide to running a server as a service runs a program. The user
decided that a page that moves into Tools leaves nothing behind: no stub page, no note that it moved,
no link back and no redirect. A list of guides that named it drops the entry. Every other link to its
old address is changed to the new one, and its search questions are keyed to the new address. A reader
who arrives from a search lands on the page that answers, and the old address is not one the site
builds.

`bun nv site --check structure` holds the five areas and the sidebar, and its `tools` part holds the
eight pages, each with a checked picture and a `covers:` list
([`testing/website-pages-are-stamped`](testing.md#testing-website-pages-are-stamped)).

- **Memory:** nothing in the language or the binary. The site carries the pictures' files, and a page
  loads only its own.

**Declined:**
- **Tool pages kept under Guides.** A guide shows how to write a program, and a reader looking for
  what the debugger does would not look there.
- **A redirect or a stub at a moved page's old address.** A moved page leaves no trace, and the site
  has no redirects (`bun nv site --check structure`).

<sub>See also [`testing/website-pages-are-stamped`](testing.md#testing-website-pages-are-stamped), [`testing/a-terminal-block-shows-what-nvs-printed`](testing.md#testing-a-terminal-block-shows-what-nvs-printed), [`testing/a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned`](testing.md#testing-a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned), [`testing/a-debugger-replay-plays-what-nvs-dap-returned`](testing.md#testing-a-debugger-replay-plays-what-nvs-dap-returned), [`testing/a-screenshot-is-taken-from-a-real-run`](testing.md#testing-a-screenshot-is-taken-from-a-real-run).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-terminal-block-shows-what-nvs-printed"></a>

## A terminal block on a website page shows commands run in a fixture and what `nvs` printed, and `bun nv site --check snippets` fails when the output changes  *(designed — owned by goal tools-website)*

`rule:testing/a-terminal-block-shows-what-nvs-printed`

A terminal block shows commands run in a fixture directory and what `nvs` printed for each, with its
exit code. A hand-written `.term` beside the fixture under `website/snippets/` lists the commands, one
per line. `bun nv site --bless` runs them in a copy of the fixture and writes the output beside it as
`.term.out`, and `bun nv site --check snippets` fails when the binary now prints something else.
`tools/nv/cmd/site.ts` § *A snippet* is the home of both formats.

A value that differs from run to run is masked in both the recording and the comparison by a fixed
pattern: a duration, a date, a trace id, a temporary path and a port. The page shows the masked value
as the binary printed it on the run that was blessed, so the reader sees real output. Only the commands
are copied by the block's copy button.

A terminal block is to a command what a snippet's `.out` is to a program
([`testing/website-pages-are-stamped`](testing.md#testing-website-pages-are-stamped)): output on a page that the binary is known to print.

- **Memory:** nothing in the language or the binary. `--check snippets` runs each block's commands once.

**Declined:**
- **A typed screen recording of a terminal.** It would be a video to regenerate, and its text could not
  be compared or searched.

<sub>See also [`testing/website-pages-are-stamped`](testing.md#testing-website-pages-are-stamped), [`testing/the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool`](testing.md#testing-the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned"></a>

## A website replay plays what `nvs lsp` returned for its steps, and `bun nv site --check` fails when the server now returns something else

`rule:testing/a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned`

A replay on a website page shows an editor session that turns one snippet's starting text into the
snippet, and every answer it shows from the language server is one `nvs lsp` returned for those steps.
A hand-written `.replay` beside the snippet lists the steps, `bun nv site --bless` writes the recording
beside it as `.replay.out`, and `bun nv site --check snippets` fails when the server now returns
something else, or when the steps do not end on the snippet's own text. `tools/nv/cmd/site.ts`
§ *A snippet* is the home of both formats.

A replay has three kinds of step: typing text one character at a time, accepting the selected
completion row, and showing the diagnostic under the cursor. A completion list is recorded wherever an
editor asks the server for one: at a trigger character
([`ide/completion-is-asked-where-a-spelling-ends`](ide.md#ide-completion-is-asked-where-a-spelling-ends)) and at the first letter of a word. Each list,
each diagnostic and each hover is recorded. Narrowing a list as more letters are typed is the editor's
own work, so the page imitates it: case-insensitive matching of the letters in order, the best match
first, the matched letters highlighted. The component's head comment says which parts are recorded
and which are imitated, and a page never presents the replay as VS Code's exact behaviour.

A replay is one panel with a look of its own, tinted with the site's accent, that holds everything
in order: a header "How it looks in your editor", a notice that says it was recorded from the editor
extension, that the reader cannot type in it, and that links to the editor install page, then the
editor window, then one button, then a collapsed section that gives the same steps as text, for
screen readers and search. The window has a title bar with the snippet's file name, and a bar along
its bottom that shows how far the replay has played. The panel's root carries Starlight's
`not-content` class, so the page's text styles add no space between the code's lines, and a list
opens on the line under the cursor, at the column where the word it completes starts. The code's font
never goes below 12px. A line wider than the window does not wrap: the code scrolls sideways, as an
editor does, so after each frame the cursor and the open list or error card are in view, and a frame
already in view does not move it. The line numbers stay in place while it scrolls.

A replay never starts by itself. Before it plays, it shows the last frame with a list open. The
button plays it from the first frame, pauses it while it plays, and plays it again from the first
frame once it has ended; its icon and its label say which it does next. Before the first play and
while paused, the label says what the recording shows: "Preview the error message" when the
recording has a diagnostic, and "Preview the autocompletion" when it has only completion lists. The
button works from the keyboard. The code never takes keyboard focus, and clicking it does nothing.
A replay pauses when its window leaves the view, plays once and stops on the last frame, and only
one replay on a page plays at a time. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the cursor does not blink and the
progress bar does not slide. Every caption and label follows AGENTS.md § *Text an end user reads*.

A recording drawn by hand would show completions the server never offers, and nothing would notice
when the server changes. Recording the server's answers and checking them on every `--check` keeps the
page honest the same way a `.out` keeps a snippet's output honest. The snippet is the replay's last
frame, so the code a page shows and the code the replay ends on cannot disagree, and a page needs no
`<Snippet>` of the same file beside it. The header, the notice, the panel's own look and the focus
rules keep a reader from mistaking the replay for an editor they can type in, or for code to copy. A
replay that plays only when asked does not move while somebody reads the text around it.

**Memory:** nothing in the language or the binary. A page pays for one small script and the
recording of each replay it shows. `--bless` and `--check snippets` start `nvs lsp` once more per
replay.

**Declined:**
- **An editor library on the page.** The frame, the list and the squiggle are plain HTML and CSS, so
  the page weight is the recording and one script.
- **Recording the narrowing of a list.** The server returns one list per request, and the narrowing
  after it is the editor's, so recording it would claim the server did work it does not do.
- **Hover cards and quick fixes as steps before a page needs them.** Each kind of step is another
  format to check, and no page shows one yet.
- **Starting when the replay scrolls into view.** Motion the reader did not ask for pulls the eye
  from the text they are reading, and the poster frame already shows the list.
- **A font that shrinks until every line fits.** On a phone the code became too small to read, and
  a long line still did not fit.
- **Buttons that step one frame back or forward.** The steps as text give the same detail, and one
  button is simpler to read.

<sub>See also [`testing/website-pages-are-stamped`](testing.md#testing-website-pages-are-stamped), [`ide/completion-is-asked-where-a-spelling-ends`](ide.md#ide-completion-is-asked-where-a-spelling-ends), [`ide/a-completion-row-reads-as-a-declaration`](ide.md#ide-a-completion-row-reads-as-a-declaration).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-replay-renames-applies-an-action-and-shows-a-lens"></a>

## A website replay can rename, apply a code action, show the code lenses, the call hierarchy and a hover card, each recorded from `nvs lsp` and checked like a completion list  *(designed — owned by goal tools-website)*

`rule:testing/a-replay-renames-applies-an-action-and-shows-a-lens`

A replay ([`testing/a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned`](testing.md#testing-a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned)) has five more kinds of step.
`rename NAME` renames the name under the cursor, and the frame shows the edit in the open file and how
many other files it changed. `action TITLE` opens the code actions at the cursor, shows their titles,
and applies the one with that title. `lens` shows the code lenses of the open file above their lines.
`calls` shows the call hierarchy at the cursor, its incoming and its outgoing calls
([`ide/the-request-set-is-closed`](ide.md#ide-the-request-set-is-closed)). `card` shows the hover at the cursor. Each answer is what
`nvs lsp` returned, recorded into the `.replay.out` in a block of its own, and
`bun nv site --check snippets` fails when the server now returns something else.

The steps still end on the snippet's own text. A rename or an action changes the text, so the snippet
is the text after the edit, and the start text is the text before it.

A rename, an action, a lens, a call hierarchy and a hover card are what the editor's own features look
like, and the Tools area shows each of them. Recording them keeps a page from showing an edit or an
answer the server does not give.

- **Memory:** nothing in the language or the binary. A page pays for the recording of each replay it
  shows.

**Declined:**
- **Showing the other files a rename changed.** The frame is one editor window, and the count says
  what the reader needs.

<sub>See also [`testing/a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned`](testing.md#testing-a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned), [`testing/the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool`](testing.md#testing-the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool), [`ide/the-request-set-is-closed`](ide.md#ide-the-request-set-is-closed).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-debugger-replay-plays-what-nvs-dap-returned"></a>

## A website debugger replay plays what `nvs dap` returned for a session's breakpoints and steps, and `bun nv site --check snippets` fails when it now returns something else  *(designed — owned by goal tools-website)*

`rule:testing/a-debugger-replay-plays-what-nvs-dap-returned`

A debugger replay on a website page shows a debug session over one snippet: where it stopped, the call
stack, and the variables with their values. A hand-written `.dap` beside the snippet lists the
breakpoints and the steps: `continue`, `next`, `in` and `out`. `bun nv site --bless` runs `nvs dap`
over the snippet, sends those requests, and writes each stop's answers to `.dap.out`: the line and the
reason, the frames by name and line, and each variable's name, type and value.
`bun nv site --check snippets` fails when `nvs dap` now returns something else.
`tools/nv/cmd/site.ts` § *A snippet* is the home of both formats.

A number that only names an object for the length of one session, such as a variables reference, is
left out of the recording, so two runs of the same session record the same file.

The panel has the replay's look and its rules for play, pause and focus
([`testing/a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned`](testing.md#testing-a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned)). The editor window shows the
breakpoint and the stopped line, and beside it are the call stack and the variables. A drawn debugger
would show values the program never had, and recording `nvs dap`'s answers is what keeps the page true.

- **Memory:** nothing in the language or the binary. `--bless` and `--check snippets` start `nvs dap`
  once per replay.

**Declined:**
- **A screenshot of VS Code's debugger.** It needs a real editor in CI, and the picture would show
  VS Code's look, which changes with every release.

<sub>See also [`testing/a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned`](testing.md#testing-a-replay-plays-what-the-language-server-returned), [`ide/the-debug-adapter-does-not-wait-for-an-editor`](ide.md#ide-the-debug-adapter-does-not-wait-for-an-editor), [`testing/the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool`](testing.md#testing-the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-screenshot-is-taken-from-a-real-run"></a>

## A website screenshot is taken by `bun nv site --shoot` from a real run, and the text beside it fails `bun nv site --check shots` when the run would now show something else  *(designed — owned by goal tools-website)*

`rule:testing/a-screenshot-is-taken-from-a-real-run`

A screenshot on a website page is taken from a real run by `bun nv site --shoot`, and nothing else
writes one. A hand-written `.shot` names an app under `apps/`, the requests to send it, and the steps
to take in the browser: open an address, click, type and wait. The command serves the app in
development with `[debug] store` on, sends the requests, starts `nvs debug`, takes the steps with
Playwright, and writes the picture beside the `.shot` with a `.shot.out`.

The `.shot.out` is what the picture shows, as text: the page's visible text with every duration, date,
trace id and port masked, and the hash of the viewer's built assets. `bun nv site --check shots` runs
the same steps and fails when the text or the hash differs. Pixels are never compared, because two
machines draw the same page with different fonts and different anti-aliasing. A change to the viewer's
look changes the hash, so the picture is taken again.

A profile's picture is the speedscope build the VS Code extension bundles, opening a real
`--profile=speedscope` export of a fixture. Speedscope is the viewer a profile is handed to
([`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact)), so the website draws no flame
chart of its own. Its `.shot.out` holds the frames and their call counts, never their times, because
times differ on every run.

- **Memory:** nothing in the language or the binary. The site carries each picture's file. `--shoot`
  and `--check shots` start a server, `nvs debug` and a browser once per run.

**Declined:**
- **Comparing pixels.** The same page differs by font rendering on each machine, so the check would
  fail on a machine that changed nothing.
- **A screenshot taken by hand.** Nothing would notice when the viewer changes.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact), [`testing/the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool`](testing.md#testing-the-tools-area-has-a-page-for-each-tool), [`observability/speedscope-timeline-export`](observability.md#observability-speedscope-timeline-export).</sub>

<a id="testing-hostile-case-contract"></a>

## A hostile case passes when nothing came apart, and a compile diagnostic is never a pass

`rule:testing/hostile-case-contract`

A hostile case is judged by a contract, never by frozen output. Its assertion is that nothing came
apart: a program that throws, one a limit stops, one that runs out of memory and says so, and one
that simply works are all passes. A panic, an abort, a hang past its timeout, a crash-shaped exit
status and a definite leak under valgrind are not.

The one failure that would otherwise look like a pass is a **compile diagnostic**, and it is checked
for by name — an attack that does not compile was never delivered, and a typo would otherwise
survive every sweep for the rest of this repository's life. Where the refusal *is* the assertion — a
sink handed a tainted value, a capability used without being granted — the case says so, and
compiling cleanly is then what fails it.

A program that **ends before its last line** is the same failure one step later: a case is several
attacks in one file, and an uncaught throw or a limit in the second of them delivers none of the
ones behind it. So every step that can be caught is caught, and a non-zero exit status fails the
case. What cannot be caught — a limit, `exit` — is the file's last step, and the case names that
step and its ending: `// hostile: ends-early <step> <ending>`. The ending is the class the error
report names for an uncaught throw, `FATAL` for a limit and `exit` for an `exit` with a non-zero
status, and the step prints `step <N>` on a line of its own as its first statement. The case passes
only when that line was printed and the program then stopped with the ending it names. Stopping
before the step, stopping with another ending, running to the last line, and a marker with no step,
no ending or a step that is not the last all fail it.

The step is the number its step comment carries (`// 4.` or `// Step 4:`), and a file with one
attack is step `1`. The `step <N>` line is how the runner knows the program reached the step: a
`FATAL` prints only its message, with no class and no frames, because no backtrace is taken on the
path that stops a program at a limit, and `exit` prints nothing. One rule for every ending is simpler
for an author than one for throws and another for the rest. Where the error report does name a line,
the runner maps the outermost frame in the attack file to the step comment above it, and a failure
names the declared and the reached together: `stopped at step 2 with RuntimeError, declares step 4
with FATAL`. An attack that stops before its last step is fixed so the step runs; moving the marker
to the step it stops in is softening the case.

Freezing the output instead is refused: every one of these programs is written to produce output
nobody can predict, and a suite whose expectations must be maintained is a suite that gets weakened
until it passes.

**Declined:**
- **The error report's line alone.** It finds the step for a throw, and a throw is the ending an
  attack should not have. A `FATAL` has no frames, so the endings that matter most would go
  unchecked.
- **A class for each limit** (`MemoryLimitError`). No such class exists, and none should exist only
  so that a marker can name it; giving a `FATAL` a class would change what every operator reads for
  the sake of a test runner.

<sub>See also [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs), [`testing/a-failing-proof-is-fixed-or-recorded`](testing.md#testing-a-failing-proof-is-fixed-or-recorded), [`testing/capability-completeness-test`](testing.md#testing-capability-completeness-test).</sub>

<a id="testing-feature-proofs"></a>

## A feature is finished when its feature proofs exist: a description, a test from both sides, three examples, a measured figure and its growth, an attack and its help in the binary

`rule:testing/feature-proofs`

A feature is finished when its **feature proofs** exist, not when it works. Each one proves a
different thing about the feature, and this list is the only place that says which they are.

**Description** — a short page of plain prose saying what the feature does, which a beginner and an
expert read the same way. It is the first thing the website shows for the feature, it is written
first, and every kind of feature owes it.
**Tests** — its behaviour pinned from Novis *and* from Rust; a `Core` member owes at least one of
each. **Examples** — three small, self-contained, plainly-commented programs a reader learns from.
**Perf** — one measured figure *and its growth*: the figure, so a change can be re-measured against
it, and the doubling ramp of `bun nv scaling` over the same bench, so a cost that grows faster than
the bench's declared `// bench: complexity` fails before it ships. The counts decide and the clock
reports; valgrind runs only when the ramp shows no clear growth, only to find the batch at which it
is clear, and never in `nv verify` or an ordinary bench run. **Hostile** — one program written to
break it, which passes when the runtime is still standing.
**Help** — the binary that runs the feature explains it. `nvs agent find` reaches the feature under
the name its user types, and `nvs agent show` prints what it does, how it is written and what it
throws or reports: a `Core` member's card, a language feature's reference section, a command's or a
configuration key's own entry. It is written with the feature and changed with it, in the voice of
AGENTS.md § *Text an end user reads*, because a user and their coding agent look there before
anywhere else, and a feature the binary cannot show them reads as one that does not exist. The
features that landed before Help was a proof are listed in `data/proofs/help-backlog.json` and read as
skips with one shared reason, so a finished goal's floor does not fail over a proof that was not owed
when it finished; a feature leaves the list when it gains its help, and nothing is ever added to it,
because a feature that lands owes its help at once.

The `about` page is owed by every feature, so no file under `data/proofs/skip/` carries an `about` skip. A
description that fails the shape check is rewritten, never padded or trimmed to fit: too long means it
explains edge cases the tests own, and too short means its lead sentence carries the page.

Each tree's own README owns what a file in it *is*, and this rule restates none of them.

**Perf's growth is judged on the counts.** The ramp judges the slope of each count's increment as the
batches double, so start-up and set-up cancel out and the verdict is the same on every machine; the
clock is reported and never fails a proof, sets an iteration count or decides that a bench is proven.
`tools/nv/cmd/scaling.ts`'s module doc is the one home of the ramp, its agreement test, its ceiling
and its bounds, and `bun nv proofs --record-perf` and `bun nv proofs --id '<feature>'` run it with no
extra command. A bench that grows past its bound is a failing proof
([`testing/a-failing-proof-is-fixed-or-recorded`](testing.md#testing-a-failing-proof-is-fixed-or-recorded)), and no ledger record is written. Every bench
declares `// bench: complexity`, and `quadratic` is never accepted; a bench with no declaration fails
its proof, so the size check cannot be skipped by omission. Callgrind runs only where the counts stay
flat while the work happens inside a Rust member and the clock is too noisy to read before the ramp
reaches its ceiling. It finds the batch at which the growth is clear, the bench's `// bench:
iterations N` is set from it with a note that callgrind measured it, and later runs do not start
valgrind again until the bench's definition changes or the ramp at N is unclear again. A bench still
unclear after callgrind is reported, not judged. Valgrind stays out of `nv verify` because callgrind
costs minutes per bench and needs WSL on Windows, so a gate that could start it would be as slow as
its slowest unclear bench. A recording sweep costs more per bench than one timed run, because the
ramp runs several batches, and that cost is paid when a figure is re-measured, not on every verify.

Not every kind of feature owes every proof: an enum is not attacked and a directive is not
benchmarked.
What each kind owes is **data**, overridable per feature, because a policy stated only in prose is a
policy nothing can check. A single feature excused from a single proof is a skip entry carrying
**the reason as its value**, so "this cannot be measured" and "nobody wrote one" never look the same
in the audit.

The proofs are a cost spent up front, per feature, and spent on security and correctness: an attack
per feature is a security question asked before a user asks it. What keeps the audit affordable to
re-run is that its gate runs no program. It checks what exists on disk, so a sweep over a finished
tree is a walk of the directories. An audit that reads mostly red is the honest number, never a
reason to loosen what a kind owes; turning one proof off for the whole roster changes what is owed
and says so in the audit.

**Declined:**
- **Line coverage instead of a test from Rust.** A coverage run says which lines ran, not which
  feature is proven, and a coverage percentage is a threshold rather than a finished feature.
- **A hand-kept checklist of finished features.** It rots within a day of an unattended run
  ([`testing/roster-is-derived`](testing.md#testing-roster-is-derived)).
- **Growth judged by one ratio of two clock figures against a scaled sibling.** A noisy machine can
  pass or fail it at random, and at a tolerance of three times the predicted ratio it misses a slope
  of 1.5: at a scale factor of 4 a linear bench may cost 12 times as much per operation, and `n^1.5`
  costs 8.
- **Callgrind on every bench.** Its verdict is exact, and it costs minutes per bench on every
  recording, for a question the counts already answer for most benches.

<sub>See also [`testing/roster-is-derived`](testing.md#testing-roster-is-derived), [`testing/proof-attribution`](testing.md#testing-proof-attribution), [`testing/member-perf-ledger`](testing.md#testing-member-perf-ledger), [`testing/hostile-case-contract`](testing.md#testing-hostile-case-contract), [`testing/one-slice-is-one-feature`](testing.md#testing-one-slice-is-one-feature).</sub>

<a id="testing-roster-is-derived"></a>

## The roster of features is read from the registry and the reference chapters, never kept as a list

`rule:testing/roster-is-derived`

The roster of features is read from live sources and kept nowhere. The registry's own machine-
readable answer names every registered class, member, exception, enum, interface and directive, so a
member that is not implemented is owed no proofs and one that lands is owed them at once. Every `#`
heading of the language and tool reference chapters names one language or tool feature, and those
chapters already state every rule the shipped compiler has, which makes their headings a roster that
maintains itself.

A source that stops naming a feature stops owing proofs for it; one that starts naming a new feature
owes them on the next sweep. Nobody edits a list, so no list is ever stale — a hand-kept roster is
wrong within a day of an unattended run, and it under-reports silently, which is the failure mode
that looks like success.

<sub>See also [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs), [`testing/proof-attribution`](testing.md#testing-proof-attribution).</sub>

<a id="testing-proof-attribution"></a>

## An example, an attack and a bench are attributed by path; a test is attributed by a marker

`rule:testing/proof-attribution`

An example, an attack and a bench are attributed by **where they sit**: the trees share one relative
path per feature, so nothing has to be registered anywhere.

A test cannot work that way — a case lives where its suite wants it, and one case often pins several
features — so a test is attributed by a comment naming what it covers, written in a `.nvst` case's
file block or above a Rust test function. For a `Core` member the scan additionally credits a case
that plainly calls it by its written `::` spelling, which is what lets the cases written before this
rule count without being rewritten.

That written spelling is the only inference made. Crediting a bare `->method(` call to every class a
case happens to name is unsound rather than merely loose, and no tightening fixes it without a type
checker.

<sub>See also [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs), [`testing/roster-is-derived`](testing.md#testing-roster-is-derived), [`testing/examples-live-in-the-repository`](testing.md#testing-examples-live-in-the-repository).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-failing-proof-is-fixed-or-recorded"></a>

## A proof that fails is fixed or recorded as a known gap, and never weakened

`rule:testing/a-failing-proof-is-fixed-or-recorded`

An attack that breaks the member it was written against, and an example that disagrees with the
binary, are the program working. There are two answers and no third.

**Fix it**, in the slice that found it, with a case pinning the corrected behaviour. This is the
default, and most findings are small. **Record it**, when the fix is genuinely larger than a slice:
a gap record under `data/gaps/` naming its owner, plus a `// proof: gap <gap id>` marker on the
proof naming that record.

A marked proof counts as a known gap rather than a failure, so a long unattended run is not stopped
by one bug it cannot fix. Two rules keep that from becoming a way to make anything green: the marker
must name a gap record that exists, so recording a bug means giving it an owner the owner gate holds
a goal to; and **a marked proof that passes fails the sweep**, so removing the marker is part of
whatever fix eventually lands.

**Weakening the proof is not one of the two.** Softening the attack, re-blessing the example or
skipping the feature each turn a finding into a green check, which is the single outcome this rule
exists to prevent. A skip is for a proof that *cannot exist*, never for one that fails.

<sub>See also [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs), [`testing/hostile-case-contract`](testing.md#testing-hostile-case-contract), [`testing/one-slice-is-one-feature`](testing.md#testing-one-slice-is-one-feature).</sub>

<a id="testing-capability-completeness-test"></a>

## Every member of a capability-bearing class declares a capability or declares none, and there is no allowlist

`rule:testing/capability-completeness-test`

A class is **capability-bearing** when any of its members has a row in the capability table. For
such a class **every member owes exactly one row**, and a member that genuinely needs no
capability — one that manipulates a string and touches no disk — declares that by entering the table
with *no capability*, rather than by staying out of it.

There is no allowlist, and that is the point. A member that is hard to classify is a member whose
capability has not been thought about, and the answer is to think about it, not to exempt it — so
the one move this design forbids is the one an exception list makes cheapest. The claim is about the
whole *set*, and a set with a growable exception list makes no claim at all. Declaring "nothing"
costs what declaring a real capability costs, is reviewed in the same table beside its reason, and
grants nothing, because no row grants anything.

A second completeness test covers the other half: nothing in the standard library reaches the operating
system except through a door. Neither test subsumes the other — one catches a member that goes
through a door undeclared, the other a member that reaches the OS with no door at all.

<sub>See also [`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs), [`testing/hostile-case-contract`](testing.md#testing-hostile-case-contract).</sub>

<a id="testing-attribution-is-diffed-in-ci"></a>

## The third-party notice is committed, and a check fails when the lockfile moved without it

`rule:testing/attribution-is-diffed-in-ci`

`bun nv gen-attribution --check` regenerates the third-party notice and compares it,
failing when the lockfile has moved and the notice has not. It runs beside the dependency-policy
job, which it completes: one decides what may be linked, this decides what must be shipped. The two
fail differently. A license the policy does not allow fails loudly the moment its dependency is added;
a missing notice fails silently, and only at distribution, unless this job catches it.

Committing a generated file is deliberate. It makes the notice reviewable in a diff at the moment a
dependency changes, and it keeps the build from depending on network access or on fetched sources.

**Declined:**
- **Generating the notice at build time instead of committing it.** Every build would depend on the
  generator and on fetched sources, and the reviewable diff, which is how a human notices a new
  component at all, would be gone.

<sub>See also [`testing/lane-table`](testing.md#testing-lane-table), [`testing/ci-lanes`](testing.md#testing-ci-lanes).</sub>

<a id="testing-debug-mode-directive"></a>

## `[debug] mode` is the ceiling as well as the default, and writing a trace or a profile is its own capability

`rule:testing/debug-mode-directive`

`[debug] mode` in `nvs.toml` states the default **and** the ceiling in one value: `[]` is off, and
any subset of `coverage`, `branch`, `trace` and `profile` is a ceiling a request may narrow and can
never widen. A production tree sets `mode = []` and no request-side call can turn any bit on.
Any other name stops the start where it is written.

`nvs run` and `nvs test` arm the probes the file names. **A server whose `[debug] mode` names
`branch`, `trace` or `profile` fails its boot and its reload**, with an error that says why, the
same on every platform. A `trace` probe files two owned strings per compiled call with no ceiling,
and nothing reads them on a served request ([`observability/four-kinds-become-a-span`](observability.md#observability-four-kinds-become-a-span)); `branch`
counts edges nothing on a server reads.

**A development server may name `coverage`**, and only `coverage`: the tree's `[mode] default` is
`development`, or the boot fails as above. Its compiler builds a located coverage table beside each
unit, and each request whose mode is `development` counts into a zeroed copy of its own, so
`Core\Debug::coverage()` names what ran and the request's spool `coverage` line carries it to the
debug viewer's heatmap ([`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact)). A
production request under the same tree counts nothing. Whether a server counts is fixed at its boot,
and a reload that would start or stop counting is refused with a message to restart. Spends one
`u64` per statement and edge and one file and line per statement per unit, once, and one `u64` per
statement and edge per development request in flight, freed with the request; nothing where the
tree names no `coverage`, which is every production host.

Whether a running request's internals are observable is not a request-local decision. An
attacker-controlled request that could turn tracing on for itself in production would gain a
reconnaissance channel over call arguments and timing, which is not a trade this language makes.

Writing a trace or a profile is its own capability — `debug.trace` and `debug.profile`, each granted
to named roots, deny-by-default, and **separate from the grant to write a file**. Being able to
write an ordinary file is not permission to persist a continuous log of every call's arguments,
which can carry request data a coverage-only deployment never needed to expose. A grant of
`debug.trace` is still a channel from request data to disk, so an operator names its roots
explicitly, the same way a path-rooted spawn grant is named. A query span rendered because `trace`
is on needs `debug.trace`; a span rendered because the request is sampled needs no grant. A run with
`trace` on and no `debug.trace` grant writes one warning per process to the diagnostic channel, at its
first query, naming the line to add, so a trace that comes out empty is never silent.

**Declined:**
- **`[debug] mode` as a directive a request may set freely.** Observability of a request's own
  internals is not a request-local decision, for the reason above.
- **Arming the probes on a server with a cap on its `call` events.** The cap would be a new limit.
- **Refusing only `trace` and `profile` on a server.** `branch` would be accepted and count nothing.
- **Counting coverage on a production server.** A table per request on every host buys a heatmap
  only a developer reads, and a production tree is the one that must arm nothing.
- **Building the coverage table on a unit's first counted request.** It would be made on first use
  on the request path; the compile that builds the unit builds it.
- **Gating a sampled request's query span on the `debug.trace` grant.** Sampling is the request to
  export ([`observability/a-query-is-a-trace-event`](observability.md#observability-a-query-is-a-trace-event)); the grant gates only a span `trace` renders.

<sub>See also [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`testing/debug-surface`](testing.md#testing-debug-surface).</sub>

<a id="testing-debug-probes"></a>

## Coverage, tracing and profiling are one per-request flag word checked at fixed probe sites, never a second compiled tier

`rule:testing/debug-probes`

`Ctx` carries one small mutable bitset — coverage, branch, trace and profile — and codegen emits an
unconditional load-and-branch against it at exactly two kinds of site, present in every compiled
unit whether or not any request ever sets a bit. At **every statement boundary**: a per-line hit
counter under coverage, and the same at every conditional edge under branch, using the edge identity
the IR already carries. At **every call site**: an entry and an exit probe under trace, carrying the
same checked-return status the call site already branches on, so a trace records a thrown or fatal
exit as it happened rather than as a reconstruction; under profile the same pair accumulates
self and inclusive time per callee.

Nothing else. No probe at expression granularity and none inside a native scalar sequence, so the
added check count is bounded by source size rather than by how many instructions a statement lowers
to.

Every bit off costs one cached load and one predicted-not-taken branch — the cost class the
safepoint poll already pays. Turning a bit on for a running request is exactly setting the word: no
recompilation, no re-resolution, no second compiled unit. That is what makes starting and stopping
coverage **mid-request** work at all, which a compiled-in-advance instrumented tier cannot do.

The probe sites are their own, not the safepoint poll's. Safepoints sit only at loop back-edges and
function entry, deliberately sparse, and line and branch counting need a site at every statement and
edge. So the probes add more checks than the poll has, each of the same cheap shape, and the
all-bits-off cost per site is a measured guard rather than an assumption. If that guard ever shows a
real regression, the fix is coarsening the site to one per basic block, never dropping the flag word.

**A compile switch of this same compiler is not a second tier.** What this rule declines is a second
compiled unit chosen per request while a program runs. The debugger's switch
([`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch)) is chosen once, when a debug
session starts, changes how the one baseline compiler lowers every unit of that session, and is never
set for a normal run. Its stop sites are separate from these probes, so a debugged request may or may
not also collect coverage, and the two are independent mechanisms.

**Declined:**
- **A second, instrumented compiled tier chosen per request.** A request's tier is fixed once it is
  resolved, so starting coverage mid-request would need frames already running to have been
  instrumented from the start. That either costs every request whether or not it asks, or leaves the
  per-test bracketing a coverage harness relies on broken.
- **Hooking a central dispatch routine, the way an interpreter's tracer does.** There is none to hook:
  typed scalar operations lower to native instructions with no common dispatch point.

<sub>See also [`testing/debug-surface`](testing.md#testing-debug-surface), [`testing/debug-mode-directive`](testing.md#testing-debug-mode-directive), [`testing/bench-counters`](testing.md#testing-bench-counters), [`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch).</sub>

<a id="testing-debug-surface"></a>

## Each probe starts and stops mid-request, and exports what existing tooling already reads

`rule:testing/debug-surface`

`Core\Debug` starts and stops each probe from inside a request — coverage with an optional branch
half, a trace to a named sink, a profile to another — and reads coverage back as a path-to-line-to-
count map. `nvs test` and `nvs run` grow flags that wrap a whole run in those calls with no source
change at all, which is the ergonomics CI uses day to day.

**The members are one start and stop pair per probe and one read-back**, so no member takes a mode
([`core-api/no-mode-strings`](core-api.md#core-api-no-mode-strings)):

```text
Core\Debug::startCoverage(bool $branches = false): void
Core\Debug::stopCoverage(): void
Core\Debug::coverage(): array<array<int>>
Core\Debug::startTrace(string $path): void
Core\Debug::stopTrace(): void
Core\Debug::startProfile(string $path): void
Core\Debug::stopProfile(): void
```

- **A start narrows within `[debug] mode` and never widens it** ([`testing/debug-mode-directive`](testing.md#testing-debug-mode-directive)).
  The ceiling is the mode plus every probe the host itself turned on, such as `nvs test`'s coverage
  flags. A start whose probe is outside it throws a `RuntimeError` naming the line to add, and turns
  nothing on. `$branches` needs `branch` as well as `coverage`. A stop always succeeds, since it only
  narrows, and it also turns off a probe the mode armed. A child context's ceiling is its parent's
  flag word at the spawn.
- **A trace or profile path is admitted under its own grant**, `debug.trace` or `debug.profile`
  ([`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes)), through the same path door `fs.write` uses, and asked before the mode.
  A second start while one sink is named throws a `LogicError`, so one probe writes one file at a time.
- **`startProfile` writes speedscope**, the timeline format; Callgrind comes from the CLI flag. One
  format per member keeps the surface small.
- **`coverage()` is path to line to count**, an `array` keyed by file path whose values are arrays
  keyed by line number. A line's count is the largest count of a statement on it, the rule the
  `nvs test` reports use, and a line that did not run is not listed, so the answer grows with the
  code that ran and not with the program. It reads the table the host installed, which holds where each
  statement is written (`nvs_runtime::StmtLines`); with no table it is empty. The declared type is
  `array<array<int>>` because Novis's array is its map type.

What comes out is what existing tooling already reads: Clover and lcov for coverage, Callgrind and
speedscope for the profile. The trace is newline-delimited JSON, because no third-party tooling widely
consumes any trace format either. A coverage report opens in the CI dashboard a project already has
configured, and a profile opens in KCachegrind, Webgrind or speedscope unmodified, so there is no client
to write. The price is four exporters to keep correct instead of one, and a low barrier to entry is
worth it.

**There is one profiler, and it is deterministic.** The call probe pair times every call and attributes
exact self and inclusive time per function. `--profile=callgrind` writes the totals and
`--profile=speedscope` the timeline ([`observability/speedscope-timeline-export`](observability.md#observability-speedscope-timeline-export)), on `nvs run` and
`nvs test` alike. The probe adds its own cost to every call, so call-heavy code reads slower in a
profile than it runs, and the profiler's docs say so. Novis builds no sampling profiler.

- **Memory:** line and branch counters are bounded by the code a request touches, not by how often a
  loop iterates, so they live in the request's arena and are dropped with it. Trace and profile data
  are call-count-proportional, so they **stream to a sink** named when they start and hold nothing in
  memory, which leaves no buffer to bound with a new limit.

A spawned isolate starts from its parent's current flag word and may only narrow it. Its own data
never merges into the parent's live state; it comes back as fields on the result, by the same
copy-out rule a value, an error and a usage figure already use. Under coverage an isolate counts
into a fresh table of its parent's shape, so the parent's `coverage()` never lists a line only the
child ran; the host adds the child's table into a run table Novis code cannot read, which is what
`nvs test`'s report counts. A trace the child leaves running is closed at its end, and the result
carries its path and any write failure. A task of the same request is not an isolate and counts
into its request's table. No `Core` member reads these fields yet. Spends one counter per statement
per isolate in flight under coverage, freed at its join.

**A profile is a file and one track per context.** `startProfile` opens a profiler with one track,
the calling context's, and writes the one file its grant names. `stopProfile` closes the file, and a
context that ends with its profile running closes it then. `--profile` installs a profiler on the
run's context, and every child context gets a track of its own in the same file, because two
contexts' calls interleave and would not nest on one track. A track other than the first writes its
events to a part file beside the profile, which is copied in and deleted once the first track closes.
Under `nvs test` each test's context has a track named for the test. A `stopProfile` inside a run
`--profile` wraps turns the probe off and leaves the run's file open.

The flags are on disk as the paragraphs above describe: `nvs test` writes lcov, Clover and Cobertura
coverage (`crates/nvs-cli/src/coverage.rs`), and `--profile` and `--profile-out` on both commands
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/profile.rs`) write either export (`nvs_runtime::Profiler`). `nvs run` has no
coverage or trace flag of its own; `[debug] mode` and `Core\Debug` turn those on.

**Declined:**
- **A sampling profiler.** It would interrupt compiled code on a timer and walk native frames on every
  target, a second profiler with platform code of its own, to remove a distortion the probe-based one
  states instead ([`observability/speedscope-timeline-export`](observability.md#observability-speedscope-timeline-export)).
- **A Novis-native coverage and profile format with a converter.** Both already have dominant
  consumers, and a conversion step is friction for every project that uses them.
- **Xdebug's own trace-file format.** Nothing beyond Xdebug's own tooling reads it widely, so
  matching it would buy no consumer.
- **Merging a child's coverage or trace into the parent's live state.** That needs mutable state
  crossing the arena boundary isolation exists to keep ([`security/isolate-shares-nothing`](security.md#security-isolate-shares-nothing)),
  and returning it on the result costs nothing new.

<sub>See also [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`testing/debug-mode-directive`](testing.md#testing-debug-mode-directive), [`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch"></a>

## Under `nvs dap` the baseline compiler runs with a debug switch: every local is in a described stack slot and every statement is a stop site

`rule:testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`

Under `nvs dap`, the baseline compiler compiles the program with one switch on, and nothing else sets
it. With the switch, every local variable lives in a stack slot that a table beside the compiled unit
describes, by its name, its declared type and the slot's place in the frame, and every statement
boundary is a stop site. A stop site tests whether it is armed, by a breakpoint on its line or by a
pending pause or step, with one load and one branch. A stopped frame's variables are read from its
slots, so the debugger shows the value each variable has at that statement.

It is one compiler with a switch, the way the probes are one compiler with a flag word
([`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes)), and not a second tier. The switch is chosen when a debug session starts
and holds for every unit that session compiles, so no request ever runs a unit of the other kind. A
normal run and a production server never set it and pay nothing. A debug session runs slower, because
every local is stored at every statement. A unit compiled with the switch is never written to the
artifact cache, whose key does not cover the switch, and a session compiles its units without reading
the cache.

A site is the statement number the coverage probe already carries, and `nvs_ir::Program::stmt_spans`
maps it to its source span, so a breakpoint's file and line resolve to the sites on that line in each
compiled unit. Under a development `nvs serve`, a recompile after an edit resolves every breakpoint again
against the new unit ([`config/an-edit-reaches-the-next-request-without-a-restart`](config.md#config-an-edit-reaches-the-next-request-without-a-restart)), so a breakpoint
outlives the edit.

Each function compiled with the switch links a frame record to its task on entry and unlinks it on
return: the function, its current stop site and its slot table. A stopped task's call stack is read from
those records and never by unwinding native frames, so the walk is the same on every platform. A
variable's value is shown as the bounded tree a dump renders ([`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations)), and
a `secret` value is redacted there as in every other rendering
([`security/redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings`](security.md#security-redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings)).

- **Memory:** per debugged task, one frame record per call in flight and one stack slot per local. A
  program compiled without the switch holds none of it.

**Declined:**
- **Deoptimising a running frame into a debug version of itself.** It needs a map from every compiled
  frame back to its source state, which is an optimising tier's machinery, and the switch gets the same
  view from the baseline compiler alone.
- **Reading variables out of the native frame through per-value location lists.** A value's register
  or slot changes within one statement and differs per target, which is far more machinery than one slot
  per local in a mode that is already slow.
- **Stopping at the safepoint poll.** The poll sits only at function entry and loop back edges, so a
  breakpoint on most lines would never be reached.
