<sub>See also [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`testing/a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree`](testing.md#testing-a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree), [`ide/the-debug-adapter-does-not-wait-for-an-editor`](ide.md#ide-the-debug-adapter-does-not-wait-for-an-editor), [`security/redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings`](security.md#security-redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree"></a>

## A stop pauses every task of the debugged request at its next stop site, suspends that request's deadlines, and leaves every other request running

`rule:testing/a-stop-pauses-the-whole-task-tree`

When a task of a debugged request or program reaches an armed stop site, every task of that request's
tree stops at its own next stop site, and the debugger is told once, with each task as a thread. A task
running on another core, started by `spawn worker`, stops the same way
([`concurrency/on-worker-runs-the-child-on-another-core`](concurrency.md#concurrency-on-worker-runs-the-child-on-another-core)). Resuming resumes the whole tree.

A stopped task parks on its own stack, the way a task waiting for I/O does, so the other requests on the
same core keep running. Under a development `nvs serve`, a breakpoint stops whichever request reaches it,
and every other request is served as usual.

While the tree is stopped, its wall-time and CPU-time limits are suspended
([`errors/on-limit`](errors.md#errors-on-limit)): the time spent stopped is added to its wall deadline, and none of it is
charged as CPU time. Without that, any stop longer than the wall limit would end the request the person
is reading. The watchdog does not take a core whose debugged request is stopped for a wedged one
([`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline)), because the core is still running
other tasks.

Each task is a thread because a thread is how DAP shows concurrent execution, so no protocol extension
is needed ([`ide/the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter`](ide.md#ide-the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter)).

- **Memory:** a stopped tree holds what it held when it stopped. Each task adds only its frame records
  ([`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch)).

**Declined:**
- **Stopping only the task that reached the breakpoint.** Its siblings would run on and change the state
  being inspected, and a join in the stopped task would find them finished.
- **Stopping the whole process or the whole core.** Other requests would wait behind one debugged
  request, and a development server would stop answering every other tab.
- **Letting the deadlines run while stopped.** A stop longer than the wall limit would end the request
  being debugged.

<sub>See also [`testing/a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch`](testing.md#testing-a-debugged-program-is-compiled-with-a-debug-switch), [`ide/the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter`](ide.md#ide-the-debugger-ui-is-as-deep-as-the-adapter), [`http-server/a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline`](http-server.md#http-server-a-wedged-core-is-detected-by-its-deadline), [`errors/on-limit`](errors.md#errors-on-limit).</sub>

<a id="testing-probes-on-is-a-tested-configuration"></a>

## The conformance suite runs with the probes on, and once per optimisation level

`rule:testing/probes-on-is-a-tested-configuration`

The conformance suite runs **at least once with coverage and tracing probes enabled**, and **once
per Cranelift optimisation level**, so neither is a shape only production ever takes.

This is not box-ticking; it is the one bug class the probe design is specifically exposed to —
instrumentation crossed with compiled code, which is where other JIT-compiled engines have
dereferenced stale caches and produced wrong results under optimisation. There is no interpreter
here to fall back to.

A suite run under one configuration cannot find these. Each case checks that Novis prints what the
rules say under that one codegen, and this bug class lives only where a probe-attached or optimised
build of the same program prints something else. The cost is CI wall-clock proportional to the added
axes, and nothing at all at run time.

CI runs the conformance suite on every leg four times: at `opt_level` `speed`, again with `nvs test
--opt-level none`, again with `nvs test --probes`, and again with `NOVIS_CHECK_TYPES` set. `--opt-level` sets the level in the test
process and, as `NOVIS_OPT_LEVEL`, in every process a case starts (`nvs_codegen::set_opt_level`). It
is a flag so that `nvs test --help` lists it. The artifact cache stays on, because a unit's key
covers the level (`crates/nvs-cli/src/cache.rs`'s `unit_key`): a unit compiled at one level is never
loaded at the other.

`--probes` turns `nvs_runtime::DebugFlags::SITES` on in every context of the test process and, as
`NOVIS_PROBES`, of every process a case starts (`nvs_runtime::probe_every_site`). Compiled code
tests the whole flags word, so every statement, branch and call site calls its probe helper, and no
helper acts on that bit: the run records nothing and writes nothing. The data is the probe helpers'
half, which their unit tests cover; the compiled half, a call at every site, is the bug class above.
A program's own `Core\Debug` probes behave as in any run, because `Core\Debug` never starts or
stops `SITES` and a host call that sets the flags keeps it. Probes change no compiled code, so the
cache needs no key for them. Request path: one relaxed load per context made, and the bit is off
outside this run. Memory: nothing.

The fourth run is the checked build (`nvs_codegen::compile_checked_types`): each typed read also
tests its value against its declared type, and a value of another type stops the process naming the
line. A case whose output is right can still read a value as another type, and only this run sees
that.

Why one bit that records nothing, and not every recording bit on with its data discarded: a
recording bit is observable. `TRACE` files query spans and warns of a missing grant, and
`COVERAGE` counts into a table a program reads, so a case that tests `Core\Debug` would print
something else. Declined: turning on `COVERAGE`, `BRANCH`, `TRACE`, `PROFILE` and `COUNT` for the
run.

<sub>See also [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`testing/the-deep-lane`](testing.md#testing-the-deep-lane), [`testing/nvst-is-separate`](testing.md#testing-nvst-is-separate).</sub>

<a id="testing-redeclaration-matrix"></a>

## Every redeclaration a subclass can write is a generated conformance cell, and every cell runs or is refused as its rule says

`rule:testing/redeclaration-matrix`

Every way a subclass or an implementor can declare a member again over its parent's is a conformance
case, generated from one table. **Each cell compiles and runs the declaration its rule names, reading a
value of its declared type, or is the compile error its rule names at the line it names.** No cell is
skipped, and none is a gap record.

The table is the module doc of `bun nv soundness` (`tools/nv/cmd/soundness.ts`), and each row cites the
rule that gives its verdict. A cell is one member kind, one type relation between the two declarations
and one path a program reaches the member by:

- **members:** a method's parameter and return, an interface method's parameter and return, a static
  method's parameter and return, `compareTo`'s parameter, an instance property (plain, promoted,
  `lateinit`, hooked, `array<T>`), a `readonly` property, a static property, and a class or interface
  constant read through `self::`, the class name and `static::`;
- **relations:** the same type, a subclass, a superclass, an unrelated class, `int` under `int|string`,
  `int` over `float`, `float` over `int`, `T` under `?T`, `?T` over `T`, a union member under the union,
  and a wider union;
- **paths:** a variable of the parent's type, of the child's type, of an interface's type, `static::`,
  an erased `object` or `mixed` access, a `property<T>` key, and a first-class callable.

`--write` writes the cells to `tests/conformance/soundness/`, one file per member kind for the cells that
run and one for the cells that are compile errors. `bun nv verify` runs `--check`, which fails when a
committed file differs from what `--write` writes, and the `.nvst` step runs the cells like any case. A
cell's expectation is the rule's verdict and is never changed to match the binary: where the rule is
wrong, the rule and the table change together. `--probe` runs each cell alone, to name the one that
fails when a whole file does.

A rule-driven suite pins what a rule says, and no case exists where no rule spoke. The matrix asks the
question for every form instead, and the checked build
([`testing/probes-on-is-a-tested-configuration`](testing.md#testing-probes-on-is-a-tested-configuration)) asks it for every typed read of every case. The
cost is CI time: the cells run with the rest of the suite.

**Declined:**
- **A skip list of failing cells.** It held the first findings while they were fixed, and a list that
  outlives its fixes is a place a regression can hide. A failing cell is a red verify.
- **Hand-written cases per relation.** The relations multiply with the member kinds and the paths, and a
  hand-written set covers the combinations someone thought of.

<sub>See also [`testing/probes-on-is-a-tested-configuration`](testing.md#testing-probes-on-is-a-tested-configuration), [`testing/nvst-is-separate`](testing.md#testing-nvst-is-separate).</sub>

<a id="testing-writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate"></a>

## `[debug] store` is off by default and can only subtract, so no run mode or log level ever turns debug records on

`rule:testing/writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate`

`[debug] store` decides whether debug records are persisted at all, is off by default, and can only
subtract — no run mode, no log level and no other directive turns it on.

It is deliberately not a reading of the run mode and deliberately not a level threshold. `[log] level`
is a legitimate operational dial whose production default is `Info` and which a tree may legally
raise to chase a bug; if the debug stream rode it, that ordinary action would silently begin
persisting complete typed dumps of request data. **A reasonable operational dial must not double as a
data-exposure switch.**

So this is a second gate read together with every ceiling already in force, and off wherever either
says off. [`testing/debug-mode-directive`](testing.md#testing-debug-mode-directive)'s reconnaissance argument does not weaken because a
second key said yes, and a tree that writes no `[debug]` block gets no debug stream at all. The key is
`RuntimeTighten`, as `[debug] mode` and `[debug] inline` are: a request may turn its own recording off,
and no code can turn it on. What it turns on is the spool
([`testing/the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk)); what a request's record holds
in `development` is [`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced)'s, and
which process starts the service is
[`testing/nvs-debug-is-the-service-and-a-development-server-starts-it`](testing.md#testing-nvs-debug-is-the-service-and-a-development-server-starts-it)'s.

With the gate on, every request records its bounded span events (`query`, `http`, `spawn`) whatever
the sampling decision, because the spool is where they go. The unbounded `call` events still need the
`trace` probe bit ([`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes)).

With the gate off nothing reaches the disk, so a debug record that survives into a deployment costs
the predicted-not-taken branch [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes) already pays and nothing further. The gate
sets no probe bit: `Ctx::records_spans` is the one reader besides the spool's writer, so a run with
`store` off has the probes of a run that writes no `[debug]` block.

<sub>See also [`testing/debug-mode-directive`](testing.md#testing-debug-mode-directive), [`testing/debug-surface`](testing.md#testing-debug-surface), [`errors/debug-dump`](errors.md#errors-debug-dump), [`errors/log-level`](errors.md#errors-log-level), [`testing/the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk), [`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced).</sub>

<a id="testing-the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk"></a>

## A debug record reaches the service through a sealed spool file that one writer owns, never over a socket

`rule:testing/the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk`

A debug record reaches the service by being written to a file the writing core owns alone, never over
a socket, and the service reads a spool file only once it has been sealed.

The application therefore opens no listener and makes no outbound connection for this: there is
nothing on the request path but a buffered append to an already-open descriptor, which is cheaper
than a socket write rather than more expensive. It is never `fsync`ed per record — that, and only
that, is what would make this cost milliseconds. Nothing is lost while the service is stopped,
because the files are simply still there when it starts.

**One file per writer, sealed by an atomic rename** at 4 MiB or 250 milliseconds after its first
record, whichever comes first. A writer is one core's thread under `nvs serve` and the one thread of
`nvs run` or `nvs test`, so it needs no lock. Per writer because the server accepts per core, and
`O_APPEND` gives an atomic offset bump and not an atomic large write, so a shared file would tear
records that a dumped object tree easily makes large enough to tear. Sealed by rename because a reader
then never has to ask whether a file is still being written. A writer with no record opens no file and
arms no timer, so an idle server costs nothing here. Deleted after ingest, so this stream needs no
rotation of its own. An unsealed file untouched for a minute is past any live writer's seal, and the
ingester reads it as sealed.

The seal interval is the latency between a dump and its appearing, which is what buys everything
above.

**Where it lives.** `debug/spool/` in the data folder, `<writer>.<n>.open` while written and
`<writer>.<n>.spool` once sealed. `<writer>` is the process id, the process start time and the thread's
index, so a restarted process never reuses a name and the writer id with the line's sequence number is
a dedupe key ([`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking)).

**What a line is.** One JSON object per line, with a `kind`: `request` (the request's outcome and,
in `development`, its input and its response,
[`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced)),
`event` (a trace event, [`observability/trace-events-carry-a-kind`](observability.md#observability-trace-events-carry-a-kind), with a `query` event's call
site id where the compiler passed one), `dump` (a `Core\Debug::dump` record's bounded tree,
[`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations)), `log` (a log record of the request, because a development
server logs to its terminal and the viewer has no file to read), `body` (a part of a recorded body too
long to be written inside its `request` line) and `dropped` (how many records the cap evicted). Every
line but `dropped` carries the trace id, so the viewer joins them. A line is at most
4 MiB; a record that would be longer is written with its tree, its fields or its bodies elided to fit,
and the elision says so. One that is still too long is counted in the next `dropped` line.

Every line has `writer`, `seq` (its number among the writer's lines, from 0), `at_us` (when it was
written, in Unix microseconds), `kind`, and `trace` (32 hex digits) on every kind but `dropped`. The
rest is the kind's. A field marked optional is left out when it has no value, and a reader takes a
missing optional field as absent, so a field added later still reads an older spool.

| `kind` | Fields |
|---|---|
| `request` | `start_us`, `duration_us`, `method`, `path` without the query, `status`; optional `span` (the server's span id, the third part of its `traceresponse`), `route`, `exception` (`class`, `message`, `file`, `line`), `input` (`query`, `headers` as name and value pairs, `body`) and `response` (`headers`, `body`) |
| `event` | `event` (`call`, `gc`, `spawn`, `query` or `http`), `label`, `start_us`, `end_us`; optional `status` and `query` (`driver`, `sql`, optional `rows` and `site`) |
| `dump` | `file`, `line`, `tree` (the dump's JSON, `null` when elided), `elided` |
| `log` | `level`, `message`, `fields` (an object, empty when elided), `elided` |
| `body` | `of` (`request` or `response`), `offset` (where its bytes start in the body); optional `text` and `base64`, as in a `body` |
| `dropped` | `records` (lost since the last `dropped` line), `files` (deleted by the cap) |

A `body` has `read`, `cut`, and optional `declared` (the length the request declared), `text` (the
bytes, when they are UTF-8), `base64` (the bytes, when they are not), `chunks` and `withheld` (the
bytes were left out because a `secret` field in them could not be found). A recorded body of
at most 64 KiB is written inside its `request` line. A longer one is written in `body` lines of at most
1 MiB each, ahead of its `request` line; its `body` then carries no bytes and says in `chunks` how many
lines do. A response body's lines are written while it is recorded, so it is never held whole. A
request body's are written when the request ends, once each `secret` field is replaced. No line
passes 4 MiB. A
response body is recorded when it is the bytes the program wrote: a file it sent is on disk already,
so its `body` has `read` false and the server reads the file once, to send it.
`nvs_runtime::spool::Line` is
the one type that writes and reads a line, and `crates/nvs-cli/tests/fixtures/debug/one-of-each.spool`
is one line of each kind as the writer writes it.

**The records are at rest, so the spool is guarded like a secret.** The spool and its directory are
created for the service's account alone, in a directory that must pass the same ownership check a
configuration file gets ([`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary)). A byte cap with oldest-first
eviction is mandatory rather than advisory, because nothing drains the spool while the service is
stopped. `[debug] spool_max`, a `System` key and 256 MiB by default, bounds one process's spool, split evenly between its
writers, and a writer past its share deletes its own oldest sealed file and writes a `dropped` line
with the count. A writer never reads another writer's files, so the cap needs no directory scan.
Because the files are the transport, a container needs none: the developer already mounts the project
directory, and the same property makes the service a viewer for a copied-down spool or a CI artifact.

- **Memory:** one write buffer per writer, held while the writer has an open file, and no queue
  anywhere. **Disk:** at most `spool_max` per process.

`nvs_runtime::spool` is the writer, and `nvs debug` the reader (`crates/nvs-cli/src/debug/ingest.rs`).
Under `nvs serve` each core runs one task that seals its file at the deadline
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/serve.rs`, `seal_the_spool`), and `nvs run` and `nvs test` seal theirs at exit.

**Declined:**
- **A socket collector with the application as its client.** It needs a bounded queue, a background
  drain, a circuit breaker, a retry window, a drop counter, a connect timeout on the request path and
  its own authentication. Every one of those exists only to survive the collector being absent or
  slow, and a file is absent-proof by construction.
- **One file per record.** It costs a create, a write, a close and a later delete per record. On
  Windows real-time antivirus scans each new file on close, and an undrained directory of small files
  takes seconds to enumerate.
- **A cap enforced across every writer's files.** Each seal would scan the directory, and the writers
  would need to agree on which file is oldest.

<sub>See also [`testing/writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate`](testing.md#testing-writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate), [`testing/debug-surface`](testing.md#testing-debug-surface), [`errors/engine-floor`](errors.md#errors-engine-floor), [`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced), [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced"></a>

## A request recorded in development keeps its method, path, query, headers, the body it read and its response, with the four credential headers and every field decoded into a `secret` property replaced before anything is written

`rule:testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`

With `[debug] store` on, a request served in `development` records its method, path, query, headers and
the body bytes the program read, up to `[limits] request_body`, and its response's status, headers and
body, up to the same `[limits] request_body`. Before the record is written, the values of `Authorization`,
`Cookie`, `Set-Cookie` and `Proxy-Authorization` are replaced with `[redacted]` in the request and the
response alike, and so is every body field the program decoded into a `secret` property. In
`production` the record holds the request's outcome, and its trace events and dumps are recorded as in
development, but no header and no body of the request or the response is.

The input is what makes a recorded request comparable with another and replayable, and what
`request-aware-editor` turns into a `Core\Test::request` case, which writes a placeholder where the
record says `[redacted]`. Those four headers are replaced by name, before anything reaches the disk,
because they carry a credential in every application, and a replayed request must not log in as the
person who sent the original. A header's name stays, so a compare shows that one was sent. The
response is what a test made from the record asserts: its status, its key headers and its body, a
JSON body compared structurally, and what the viewer's compare view diffs between two requests.

**The response body is capped at `request_body`.** `max_output` has no default cap, so it cannot bound
a record, and the request body's own cap already exists. A longer response body is cut at the cap with
a marker, and a test made from that record asserts only the status and the headers. The body is
written through to the spool file as the program writes it, so it is never held whole in memory.

**The body is what the program read.** The server streams a body to the program one chunk at a time
and reads nothing the program did not ask for (`crates/nvs-server/src/body.rs`), and recording does not
change that: the record keeps each chunk the program pulled, up to `request_body`, and says how many
bytes the request declared. A body the program never read is recorded as not read. Reading the rest
of the body to record it would change what the server does under the debugger, and a large upload would
be held twice.

**A body decoded into a class keeps its `secret` fields off the disk.** When the handler reads the body
through `Core\Request::jsonAs<X>()` or `postAs<X>()`
([`routing/a-request-body-is-read-from-the-handlers-own-call`](routing.md#routing-a-request-body-is-read-from-the-handlers-own-call)), the decoder knows which field lands
in a `secret` property of `X` ([`security/secret-qualifier`](security.md#security-secret-qualifier)), and the record replaces that field's
value with `[redacted]` in the stored body. A body the program read any other way is stored as it
arrived, so a password in a development login form read as raw bytes is on disk until the index forgets
it ([`testing/the-debug-index-holds-what-the-viewer-reads-for-a-bounded-time`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-index-holds-what-the-viewer-reads-for-a-bounded-time)), in a directory only
the service's account can open. The `nvs debug` reference page says so. A `jsonAs` or `postAs` that
throws replaces the fields as well, because the bytes it read are recorded either way. Where those
fields cannot be found, the record keeps no byte of the body and says `withheld`: a body that is not
one JSON document or nests deeper than 128 levels, a multipart form, and a class that writes its own
decoder, each where `X` can reach a `secret` property.

A derived codec refuses a `secret` property ([`security/derived-codec-qualifiers`](security.md#security-derived-codec-qualifiers)), so a class
`jsonAs` or `postAs` decodes reaches one only as a skipped property, which takes no value from the
body. A whole JSON document read that way is therefore stored as it arrived, and the replacement runs
on no field of it. A class that reaches a skipped `secret` property still withholds a body whose
fields cannot be found.

- **Memory:** per recorded request, the bytes the program read, up to `request_body`, held until the
  request's record is written at its end. The response body is written through to the spool, so it
  adds one write's bytes at a time. A request with the gate off holds nothing more.

**Declined:**
- **Recording input or a response body in production.** A production request's body is a customer's
  data, and the spool is a debugging aid. The mode, not a second key, decides it. The outcome, the trace
  events and the dumps are what a production incident needs, and they carry no body.
- **Redacting a body field by its name, such as `password`.** A list of names misses the field an
  application named its own way, and the `secret` property is where the program already says which
  value is a credential.
- **Replacing a credential with a hash.** A hash of a short token is a token, so a dictionary turns
  the record back into the credential.

<sub>See also [`testing/writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate`](testing.md#testing-writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate), [`testing/the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk), [`testing/the-debug-index-holds-what-the-viewer-reads-for-a-bounded-time`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-index-holds-what-the-viewer-reads-for-a-bounded-time), [`http-server/an-upload-is-received-only-through-files`](http-server.md#http-server-an-upload-is-received-only-through-files), [`routing/a-request-body-is-read-from-the-handlers-own-call`](routing.md#routing-a-request-body-is-read-from-the-handlers-own-call), [`security/secret-qualifier`](security.md#security-secret-qualifier).</sub>

<a id="testing-nvs-debug-is-the-service-and-a-development-server-starts-it"></a>

## `nvs debug` runs the debug service for one data folder, and a development `nvs serve` with `[debug] store` on starts it and stops it on exit

`rule:testing/nvs-debug-is-the-service-and-a-development-server-starts-it`

`nvs debug` runs the debug service — the ingester and the viewer — for one data folder, and a
development `nvs serve` with `[debug] store` on starts it as a child process and stops it when the
server exits. It also runs by hand, for a spool that `nvs run`, `nvs test` or a copied-down directory
filled, and `nvs debug --once` reads what is ready, applies the deletion window and exits.

One service per data folder, because the index has one writer
([`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking)). The service holds
`debug/service.lock` in the data folder for as long as it runs. A server that finds the lock held uses
the running service and does not stop it on exit; a server that started its own stops it on exit, and
the child also exits within one ingest pass of noticing its parent is gone, so a killed server leaves
no service behind on any platform. Spool files written while no service ran wait for the next one.
The service reads `[debug] index_age` and `index_max` from the configuration of the server that started
it, and from the working directory's when it is run by hand, as every command does.

The server starts the child before it binds a socket, so the child holds no listener. It runs `nvs
debug --parent`, a hidden flag, with the server's `--data` and `--config`, and a pipe as its standard
input. The pipe is how the child knows its parent is gone: the server closes it on exit, and every
platform closes it when the server dies, however it dies. A `--parent` child that finds the lock held
exits quietly, which is how the server uses the running service. The server prints one line saying
the service reads its records into the index.

A production server never starts it: a host that records with `store` on runs `nvs debug` itself, where
and when its operator chooses. The service's listener, its port and its token are the viewer's
([`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact)).

- **Memory:** the service is its own process, so a server holds nothing for it but the child's handle
  and its pipe. The child spends one thread blocked on its standard input.

**Declined:**
- **The service inside the server process.** Ingesting would scan directories and write the index on a
  core that serves requests ([`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking)).
- **One service per server.** Two ingesters would write one index.
- **A `--parent <pid>` the child polls.** It needs a liveness check per platform, and a process id can
  be reused by another process once the server is gone. A pipe needs neither.
- **The server checks the lock before it starts the child.** The lock can change hands between the
  check and the child's start, so the child has to handle a held lock anyway.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking), [`testing/writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate`](testing.md#testing-writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate), [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact).</sub>

<a id="testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking"></a>

## The ingester owns every write to the index and runs without a browser, and the viewer only ever reads

`rule:testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`

The ingester owns every write to the index and runs from the moment the service starts, whether or
not a browser has ever connected; the viewer is a reader that never opens a log file, parses a line
or scans a directory.

That split is both the performance argument and the correctness one. The viewer's worst case is a
bounded indexed query, so no enormous or corrupt file can reach the UI; and draining the spool is not
an effect of somebody having a tab open. Putting the ingester inside the application process is
refused: it would put directory scanning and index writes on the request path, in every deployment,
to save a hop that costs nothing.

**Two ingest modes.** A spool file is read to its end, inserted, and deleted. A log file named with
`nvs debug --tail <file>` is read from a checkpoint, inserted, and never touched — the checkpoint keyed
on the file's identity plus its offset plus a hash of its first line, because a path misses a rotation
and an identity alone misses identity reuse and truncation in place. Every record carries a **dedupe
key** under a unique index and inserts ignoring conflicts, so re-ingesting anything is harmless: the
writer's id and sequence for a spool record, the file identity and byte offset for a tailed one.

A tailed file is read in the `json` log format, and a line in any other is an `unparseable` record.
Its last line is read once it has a newline, since the writer may be partway through it. The
checkpoint and the rows it moves past are committed in one transaction. When the file at the path is
no longer the checkpoint's, the rest of `<file>.1`, the name a Novis log is rotated to, is read
first if that file is the checkpoint's, so the lines written just before a rotation are kept; the
new file is then read from its start. `crates/nvs-cli/src/debug/tail.rs` is the tailer.

The ingester lists the spool directory every 250 milliseconds, the seal age, while files arrive, and
every two seconds once none has arrived for a minute. A listing of an empty directory is the whole cost
of an idle service.

The order is read, insert, commit, **then** delete. A crash in that window re-ingests, which the
dedupe key makes a no-op. **The index is a cache of what was recorded**: losing it loses history and
never correctness, which is what licenses running it in its fastest mode — write-ahead logging, so the
one writer and the readers do not block each other, and synchronous writes off — and makes a corrupt
index a file to discard rather than a failure to resolve. The documented risk of that mode is
corruption rather than lost transactions, so the viewer offers discarding the index as an action, and a
tailed file is then read again from its start.

**The viewer is pushed a watermark, not records** — a monotonic sequence published after each
committed batch, with the browser fetching the delta through the same query path it uses for
everything else. One rendering path serves live and historical data, a backgrounded tab cannot make
the ingester buffer, and a browser that was closed needs no replay buffer. That sequence, not a
record's own timestamp, orders the live view, which makes it immune to clock skew between writers and
to a garbage timestamp in a corrupt file.

- **Memory:** one line at a time, of at most 4 MiB, and one open transaction per file, bounded by
  [`testing/a-bad-line-degrades-and-a-bad-file-is-quarantined`](testing.md#testing-a-bad-line-degrades-and-a-bad-file-is-quarantined)'s work per source.

The ingester is `nvs debug` (`crates/nvs-cli/src/debug.rs`): it raises the watermark in the index's
`meta` table with each batch. The viewer, its push of the watermark and its action that discards the
index are [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact)'s.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk), [`testing/a-bad-line-degrades-and-a-bad-file-is-quarantined`](testing.md#testing-a-bad-line-degrades-and-a-bad-file-is-quarantined), [`errors/log-write`](errors.md#errors-log-write), [`testing/the-debug-index-holds-what-the-viewer-reads-for-a-bounded-time`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-index-holds-what-the-viewer-reads-for-a-bounded-time), [`testing/nvs-debug-is-the-service-and-a-development-server-starts-it`](testing.md#testing-nvs-debug-is-the-service-and-a-development-server-starts-it).</sub>

<a id="testing-the-debug-index-holds-what-the-viewer-reads-for-a-bounded-time"></a>

## The debug index is one SQLite file whose tables hold every query the viewer makes, full-text search and exception groups included, and it forgets a request past `[debug] index_age` or `[debug] index_max`

`rule:testing/the-debug-index-holds-what-the-viewer-reads-for-a-bounded-time`

The index is one SQLite file, `debug/index.sqlite` in the data folder, whose tables hold every query
the viewer makes, and the ingester deletes what is older than `[debug] index_age` or past `[debug]
index_max`, the oldest request first.

| Table | One row per | What the viewer reads it for |
|---|---|---|
| `requests` | recorded request: trace id, start, duration, method, route, path, status, query, dump and log counts, its exception group | the request list and its filters |
| `inputs` | request recorded with its input: query, headers, body, bytes declared, whether the body was read, and the response's headers and body | compare, replay and a test made from the request ([`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced)) |
| `body_parts` | `body` line: trace id, request or response, offset, bytes | a body too long for its `request` line, read in offset order |
| `events` | trace event: trace id, kind, label, start, end, status, a `query` event's driver, SQL, rows and call site id | a request's timeline |
| `dumps` | dump: trace id, file, line, the bounded tree | a request's dumps |
| `logs` | log record: trace id where it has one, level, message, fields, source file and offset for a tailed line | the log view |
| `exceptions` | uncaught exception: trace id, class, message, file, line, group | a request's error |
| `exception_groups` | class and throw site: count, first seen, last seen | grouped exceptions |
| `search` | searchable text of one row above, with its table and row id | full-text search |
| `dropped` | `dropped` line: the records and files a writer's share of the spool cap deleted | what was lost before it was read |
| `unparseable`, `quarantine` | [`testing/a-bad-line-degrades-and-a-bad-file-is-quarantined`](testing.md#testing-a-bad-line-degrades-and-a-bad-file-is-quarantined)'s records | what was not read |
| `checkpoints`, `meta` | tailed file's checkpoint; the watermark and the schema version | the ingester itself |

**An exception group is a class and the file and line that threw it,** never the message, because a
message carries values and would split one bug into a group per value. A group's count, first seen
and last seen are updated as each exception is inserted, so the grouped view is one indexed read.

**Search is one FTS5 table** over a request's path and route, a dump's rendered text, a log message, a
query's SQL and an exception's class and message. Each row names the table and row it came from in
its rowid, the source row's id times eight plus the table's code, and a trigger on each table writes
and deletes its search rows. FTS5 is in the SQLite that `rusqlite`'s bundled build already
compiles, so search costs no new dependency. A secret is already redacted in every record before it is
written ([`security/redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings`](security.md#security-redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings)), so search cannot find one.

**The deletion window.** `[debug] index_age`, `7d` by default, is the oldest record kept, measured
from a request's start, and `[debug] index_max`, 1 GiB by default, is the most bytes of pages in use;
a page a deletion frees is reused, so the file stays near that size. Both are `System` keys. After
each batch the ingester deletes requests past either bound with every row that names their trace id,
in batches of a thousand so the viewer never waits on a long write. A row that names no recorded
request is deleted by its own time past `index_age`. An exception group stays while its last seen is
within `index_age`, and its count still counts deleted requests. A saved filter is the viewer's own
and is not in the index, because discarding the index must lose nothing a person wrote.

A schema version in `meta` that the running binary does not know is a cache miss: the file is
discarded and rebuilt from what is still on disk
([`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking)). So is a file SQLite cannot read.

- **Disk:** at most `index_max`. **Memory:** SQLite's page cache in the service process, never in a
  server.

**Declined:**
- **Grouping exceptions by message.** One bug that puts an id in its message would show as a group per
  id.
- **Keeping the index until a person clears it.** Recorded bodies and dumps hold request data, and a
  debugging aid that keeps them forever is a store of personal data nobody chose to keep.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking), [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact), [`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced), [`security/redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings`](security.md#security-redaction-reaches-the-tools-own-renderings).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-bad-line-degrades-and-a-bad-file-is-quarantined"></a>

## A malformed line becomes a visible record and an unreadable file is quarantined under a backoff, so ingestion never stops

`rule:testing/a-bad-line-degrades-and-a-bad-file-is-quarantined`

A malformed line becomes a record that says so and an unreadable file is quarantined under a backoff,
so nothing on disk can stop the ingester.

Line length is capped at 4 MiB, the longest line a spool writer writes
([`testing/the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk)), and past the cap the line is
truncated, marked, and skipped to the next newline. A corrupt file is often one enormous line with no
newline in it, and reading it whole is how a log tailer dies.

A line that will not parse is kept as an `unparseable` record carrying its file, its offset and its
first 4 KiB, and is shown. Dropping it silently would leave a viewer quietly disagreeing with what is
on disk, which is worse than an ugly row. Invalid UTF-8 is a lossy conversion with a flag, never an
error.

A file that fails at the file level — permissions, an IO error, a mount that went away — is
quarantined with its error and a retry-after, never retried hot, and listed in the UI, so a file that
stopped being read says so instead of merely not appearing. The first retry is after one second and
each next one doubles, up to five minutes. Other files keep flowing.

Work is bounded per source per pass, at 16 MiB, and sources are taken in turn, so one enormous file
cannot starve the live spool. A disk that is full or an index that errors backs off on the same
schedule rather than spinning, and never deletes a spool file whose batch did not commit.

What that comes to in the ingester (`crates/nvs-cli/src/debug/ingest.rs`, `crates/nvs-cli/src/debug.rs`):

- **A cut line** is an `unparseable` row with its whole length beside its first 4 KiB.
- **A spool line that is not UTF-8** is an `unparseable` row with the flag, and is never inserted as a
  record: the writer writes UTF-8 alone, so such a line is damaged. A tailed log line that is not
  UTF-8 is converted and inserted as a log record with the flag, because another program may have
  written it.
- **The budget** is passed only to finish the line a pass is in. A spool file the budget stopped in
  is committed as far as it was read, is not deleted, and goes on where it stopped in the next pass.
- **A quarantined file** is a `quarantine` row: its path, its error, its failures in a row and its
  next try. The row goes once the file is read or is gone, never by age, because a file that still
  fails must still be listed. A spool directory that cannot be listed is quarantined the same way.
- **A file that cannot be deleted** after its batch committed is quarantined too: its next read adds
  nothing, under the dedupe key, and then deletes it.

- **Memory:** one 64 KiB read buffer and one line of at most 4 MiB while a file is read; one entry per
  file failing.

The viewer showing `unparseable` and `quarantine` is [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact)'s.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking).</sub>

<a id="testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact"></a>

## The viewer renders the correlated request stream and hands every artifact with an existing viewer to it

`rule:testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`

The viewer renders the correlated request stream and the log, and every artifact that an existing
tool already renders is handed to that tool rather than drawn.

It is held to the standard of a tool every developer keeps open all day: it is the window a Novis
developer watches their program through, so it is fast at any size of index, works from the keyboard
alone, and never shows a value in a way that runs it. A view that is slow, a list that jumps while it
is read, or a link that stops working after a restart is a bug in this rule's sense, not a polish item.

A profile is handed to speedscope in the format [`observability/speedscope-timeline-export`](observability.md#observability-speedscope-timeline-export)
already commits to, and a coverage report to whatever reads Clover or lcov. A coverage **heatmap**
over source is drawn, because that is a per-line background over text rather than a viewer. This is
[`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has)'s test applied rather than set aside:
where a renderer exists, feed it. The live, correlated request stream is the one thing here that has
no incumbent in any ecosystem, which is the whole of the exception. The boundary is written as a rule
because the failure mode of an in-house dashboard is that it slowly grows a second copy of every tool
the project deliberately did not build.

**The request is the primary object.** The main view lists requests — method, route, status,
duration, query count, dump count and whether it threw — and one opens to its own timeline: the
calls, queries, spawns, garbage-collection pauses, dumps and log lines of that request on one time
axis. The flat filterable stream and the application's log are the second and third views, not the
front page. A request is keyed by its trace id and the span id the server drew for it
([`observability/a-trace-id-exists-for-every-request`](observability.md#observability-a-trace-id-exists-for-every-request)), because an inbound `traceparent` can give
two requests one trace id. The response carries both in its `traceresponse` header unless
`[trace] response_header = false`, so pasting that header's value, or a bare trace id, into the
viewer's search opens the request it names.

**The baseline every view has.** The live view follows new records and pauses at a keystroke or
when the developer scrolls away from the newest row, and a paused view counts what arrived without
moving what is on screen. Every view and every request has a link that survives a restart of the
service and a reload of the tab: `/requests/<trace id>/<span id>`, and a filter is part of its view's
link. Every action is reachable from the keyboard, `?` lists the keys, and lists and value trees
follow the WAI-ARIA listbox and tree patterns. A dark and a light theme follow the browser's
`prefers-color-scheme` and can be fixed in the viewer's settings, both at WCAG AA contrast. A long list
keeps only the rows on screen in the DOM, so the browser's cost does not grow with the index.

Four features complete it, each with its own rule: full-text search with saved filters
([`testing/the-viewer-searches-every-record-and-saves-a-filter`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-searches-every-record-and-saves-a-filter)), exceptions grouped by class and
site ([`testing/an-exception-is-one-row-per-class-and-site`](testing.md#testing-an-exception-is-one-row-per-class-and-site)), comparing two requests and replaying
one ([`testing/two-requests-compare-and-a-replay-asks-first`](testing.md#testing-two-requests-compare-and-a-replay-asks-first)), and every `file:line` opening in the
editor ([`testing/a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor`](testing.md#testing-a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor)).

The value tree the browser receives is already finite — [`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations) bounded
it with elision and resolved every repeat to an identity before it was written — so a repeat renders
as a link to the node it names and expansion needs no fetch. Children are built from data already
loaded.

**The front end is TypeScript and Solid**, in the repository's top-level `viewer/` folder, a Bun
workspace of the root package so the root `bun.lock` pins it. `solid-js` is its one runtime
dependency, at a caret range. Bun bundles it into one JavaScript file and one CSS file, with a
bundler plugin running Solid's JSX preset at build time, because Bun's own JSX transform has only the
React-style runtimes. The two files are committed under `viewer/dist/`, `bun nv viewer --check`
rebuilds them and fails on any byte difference, and the crate that serves `nvs debug` embeds them with
`include_bytes!`. A Rust build therefore never runs Bun, and the bytes in a binary are the reviewed
ones. Solid's licence is reproduced in the notice the binary carries
([`packaging/the-third-party-notice-is-generated-never-written-by-hand`](packaging.md#packaging-the-third-party-notice-is-generated-never-written-by-hand)). A second runtime
dependency is a change to this rule, because each one ships in every binary.

The browser talks to one JSON API on the same listener. The Rust side owns its shapes: a test writes a
fixture from a real index, the TypeScript types are checked against that fixture by `tsc`, and the
browser tests run against it, so the two halves cannot drift without a failing build.

**The listener is the service's own.** The viewer is a subcommand, `nvs debug`, binds
`127.0.0.1:8137` by default, a fixed port so a link outlives a restart, and is never mounted on the
application's listener: there every path-normalization bug and proxy misconfiguration would become
disclosure, and a reserved path prefix would collide with the compile-time route table. `[debug]
listen` and `nvs debug --listen` move it. A taken port stops a service started by hand with a message
naming both; a service a development server started with `--parent` says the same as a warning and
ingests on without the viewer, because the server's records still need it. It is `hyper` and
`rustls`, both already in the binary, so it adds no HTTP or TLS crate. `nvs debug` has no core, so each
connection has a thread of its own whose reads and writes block, bounded in count, in read time and in
write time, and `hyper` is driven by `nvs_host::block_on`. `half_close` keeps `hyper` from reading
while it writes, so an event stream waits on the watermark alone. The page is one `<div id="app">`
with `/viewer.css` and `/viewer.js`, served for every path outside `/api/`.
`crates/nvs-cli/src/debug/listen.rs` is the listener.

**Off loopback, `nvs debug` secures itself.** `[debug] listen` is the one key a container needs. With
an address off loopback, `nvs debug` generates a self-signed certificate with `rcgen`, already in the
graph, and a random token, keeps both in the data folder's `debug/` directory, private to the
service's account, and prints a URL that carries the token. The browser warns about the certificate
once. `[debug] tls_cert_file`, `tls_key_file` and `token_file` are optional overrides for someone who
brings their own, and boot does not fail when they are absent. The token is accepted once from the
printed URL and then lives in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie, and a request without
that cookie is refused. A bind off loopback never serves plain HTTP and never serves without a token.
`crates/nvs-cli/src/debug/secure.rs` makes and loads the certificate and the token.

Because it is a browser-facing local listener, `Host` and `Origin` are
allowlisted against DNS rebinding. On loopback a `Host` names `localhost` or a loopback address with
the bound port. Off loopback a published port and a container's name change the host a browser uses,
so any well-formed `Host` passes and the token cookie decides, which a rebound name never carries. An
`Origin` that is sent must be the page's own, a request that changes anything needs one and a
JSON body, and every page is sent with a `Content-Security-Policy` that admits no inline script, no
inline style, no `eval` and no other origin. Its renderer builds DOM rather than assigning markup: no
value from a record reaches `innerHTML`, and Solid's compiled templates are constant strings fixed at
build time. It runs no Novis code.

The viewer is pushed a watermark as server-sent events on `/api/events`
([`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking)): the ingest loop publishes the
last committed batch after every pass that read something, and a stream sends the newest number it
has not sent, or a comment every 15 seconds so a closed tab is found. Every list is a page keyed on
that sequence, so reading the newest page costs the same with a hundred requests in the index as with
a million.

The viewer's settings — the theme, the editor link, path mappings and saved filters — are one file
beside the index in the data folder, outside the index, so discarding and re-ingesting the index keeps
them, and a restart on the same port finds them.

- **Memory:** the two bundled files are read-only data in every binary, and a server process never
  pages them in, because only `nvs debug` reaches them. `nvs debug` holds one read connection to the
  index, one thread per open connection up to 64, and one sequence number per open tab. The browser
  holds one page of rows and the request it shows.

**Not on disk.** The listener serves the page, the two files and `/api/events`, and every other
`/api/` path is a `404`: the JSON API, its fixture, the views, search, grouping, compare, replay and
the settings file are not built. The one hand-off built is the editor's: the VS Code extension reads
the lcov file `nvs test` writes (`editors/vscode/src/tests.ts:237`).

**Declined:**
- **Fetching a value tree lazily as the developer expands it.** The tree is already bounded before it
  is written, so a fetch per expansion would add round trips and server-side state to make a bounded
  thing safe again.
- **Building the bundle from a Cargo build script.** Every Rust build, on every CI leg and every
  contributor's machine, would need Bun and the viewer's dependencies installed.
- **A second runtime dependency for a virtual list, a chart or a component kit.** Each one ships in
  every binary and widens what the notice and the audit cover. The viewer draws them with Solid.
- **A WebSocket for the watermark.** The push is one integer in one direction, and server-sent events
  carry it over the same HTTP connection with no upgrade and no framing to keep correct.
- **A port chosen at random on each start.** Every link and every open tab would break on a restart.

<sub>See also [`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has), [`observability/speedscope-timeline-export`](observability.md#observability-speedscope-timeline-export), [`observability/a-trace-id-exists-for-every-request`](observability.md#observability-a-trace-id-exists-for-every-request), [`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations), [`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking), [`testing/the-viewer-searches-every-record-and-saves-a-filter`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-searches-every-record-and-saves-a-filter), [`testing/an-exception-is-one-row-per-class-and-site`](testing.md#testing-an-exception-is-one-row-per-class-and-site), [`testing/two-requests-compare-and-a-replay-asks-first`](testing.md#testing-two-requests-compare-and-a-replay-asks-first), [`testing/a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor`](testing.md#testing-a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor), [`packaging/the-third-party-notice-is-generated-never-written-by-hand`](packaging.md#packaging-the-third-party-notice-is-generated-never-written-by-hand).</sub>

<a id="testing-the-viewer-searches-every-record-and-saves-a-filter"></a>

## The viewer searches the text of every request, dump, log line, query and exception, and a search can be saved and linked

`rule:testing/the-viewer-searches-every-record-and-saves-a-filter`

One search box searches the text of every request, dump, log line, query and exception in the index,
and any search can be saved under a name and opened again from a link.

The text is an SQLite FTS5 index the ingester fills as it commits each batch, so a search is one
indexed query and the viewer never scans records. FTS5 is compiled into the SQLite Novis already
bundles, so it adds no dependency. What is indexed is the record after
[`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations), so a `secret` value is already a redacted node and is not
searchable, and a value the record elided is not either.

Words match as words, a quoted phrase matches as a phrase, and a field term narrows the search:
`status:500`, `method:POST`, `route:`, `kind:query`, `level:error`, `duration:>200ms` and
`trace:<id>`. A pasted `traceresponse` value is a `trace:` term. Results come newest first, are
grouped by the request they belong to, and open that request's timeline at the matching record. The
search is part of the view's link, so a search is shared by copying the address.

A saved filter is a name and a search. It is listed beside the views, opens with its own link, and is
kept in the viewer's settings file, outside the index, so discarding the index keeps it.

- **Memory:** the FTS5 index lives on disk beside the records it indexes, and grows with them under
  the spool's byte cap and the index's deletion window. A search holds one page of results.

**Declined:**
- **A regular-expression search.** It cannot use an index, so its cost grows with every record kept.
- **Searching a parameter value of a query.** Parameters are where request data sits, and the query's
  text with its placeholders already finds the call.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact), [`testing/the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking`](testing.md#testing-the-ingester-runs-whether-or-not-anyone-is-looking), [`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations), [`packaging/a-c-dependency-answers-two-questions`](packaging.md#packaging-a-c-dependency-answers-two-questions).</sub>

<a id="testing-an-exception-is-one-row-per-class-and-site"></a>

## The viewer groups exceptions into one row per class and throw site, with its count, first and last time, and its requests

`rule:testing/an-exception-is-one-row-per-class-and-site`

The exceptions view shows one row per exception class and throw site, with how many times it was
thrown, when it was first and last thrown, and links to the requests that threw it.

A site is the file and line of the `throw` that raised it, as the record's first frame names it. The
row shows the class, the message of the latest throw, the site as a link into the editor
([`testing/a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor`](testing.md#testing-a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor)), the count, the first and last time, a small
chart of the count over time and the routes it was thrown under. Opening a row lists its requests
newest first, and each opens to its timeline at the throw. The grouping is a column the ingester
writes with the record, so the view is one indexed query.

An edit that moves the `throw` to another line starts a new row. The rows describe the code that
ran, and the index keeps them only as long as its deletion window, so an old row ages out with its
requests.

- **Memory:** one group key per exception record, on disk in the index.

**Declined:**
- **Grouping by the throwing function instead of the line.** Two different `throw` statements of one
  class in one function would share a row, and the row could not say which one ran.
- **Marking a group resolved or ignored.** That is state an index rebuilt from the files would lose,
  and the deletion window already ends a row that stops recurring.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact), [`testing/a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor`](testing.md#testing-a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor).</sub>

<a id="testing-two-requests-compare-and-a-replay-asks-first"></a>

## The viewer compares two requests side by side, and resends a recorded request to the development server only after the developer confirms

`rule:testing/two-requests-compare-and-a-replay-asks-first`

Two requests open side by side with what differs marked, and a recorded request is sent again to the
development server only after the developer confirms it in a dialog that names what will be sent.

**Compare** sets the recorded input of each — method, path, query, headers and body — against the
other, then the response — its status, headers and body, a JSON body compared structurally — the
duration, the queries in the order they ran with their text aligned, the dumps and the log lines. A second request is picked by marking it in any list, and a request's own
view offers the previous request to the same route. A redacted header shows as redacted on both
sides, never as a difference.

**Replay** sends the recorded method, path, query, headers and body to the development `nvs serve`
that started this service, and to nothing else: the target is the address that server gave its child,
never a value from the browser, so the action cannot be turned into a request to another host. A
service started by hand has no target, and the action says so. The dialog names the method, the full
path and the target, opens with the cancel button focused, and asks every time, because a replay runs
the handler's side effects again. A header the spool redacted is listed in the dialog with an empty
field: a value typed there is sent once and is never written anywhere. The replayed request gets its
own trace id, and the viewer opens it beside the original in the compare view.

Replay is a request that changes something, so it needs an allowed `Origin`
([`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact)).

- **Memory:** a replay holds one recorded request's input, under the spool's own body cap, while it is
  sent.

**Declined:**
- **Replaying to a URL the developer types.** A browser-facing listener that sends requests where it
  is told is a request forger for any page that reaches it.
- **A setting that stops the dialog asking.** The cost of one keystroke is smaller than the cost of a
  repeated payment or a repeated email.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact), [`testing/the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk`](testing.md#testing-the-debug-stream-reaches-the-service-through-the-disk), [`testing/writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate`](testing.md#testing-writing-a-debug-record-to-disk-is-its-own-gate).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor"></a>

## Every `file:line` the viewer shows opens that line in the developer's editor, VS Code by default

`rule:testing/a-site-in-the-viewer-opens-in-the-editor`

Every `file:line` the viewer shows is a link that opens that line in the developer's editor, through
the editor's own URL scheme, and VS Code's `vscode://file/` is the default.

The viewer's settings offer presets for VS Code, VS Code Insiders, VSCodium, Cursor, Zed and the
JetBrains IDEs IntelliJ IDEA and PhpStorm, and a template with `{file}`, `{line}` and `{column}` for
any other editor. A template's scheme is never one that runs or embeds content in the viewer's page
(`javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`, `blob:`): the service refuses to save one, and the viewer builds
no link from one. A list of path mappings rewrites a prefix before the link is built, the longest
that matches, for a program that ran in a container, a virtual machine or WSL and recorded paths the
editor's machine does not have. The setting is the developer's, not the project's, so it lives in the
viewer's settings file and never in `nvs.toml`.

A link is built only from a site the record carries as structured data — a frame, a query's call site,
a dump's or a log call's location — and never from text found inside a message, so a logged string
cannot make a link. A profile the timeline names opens in VS Code's *View Profile* view through the
extension's own `vscode://novis-lang.nvs/` link when the editor is VS Code, and is offered as a download
otherwise.

**Declined:**
- **Opening the file from the service with a command line.** The service would run a program a
  browser asked it to run, which is exactly what a local listener must never do.
- **Linking `file:line` text found in a log message.** Its path is whatever the message says, and the
  structured site is already there for every record that has one.

<sub>See also [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact), [`testing/an-exception-is-one-row-per-class-and-site`](testing.md#testing-an-exception-is-one-row-per-class-and-site), [`ide/the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has`](ide.md#ide-the-extension-builds-no-ui-the-editor-already-has).</sub>

<a id="testing-a-recorded-request-becomes-a-test"></a>

## `nvs debug to-test` prints a `Core\Test::request` case from a recorded request that asserts its status, key headers and body, with a placeholder where the spool redacted a credential  *(designed — owned by goal request-aware-editor)*

`rule:testing/a-recorded-request-becomes-a-test`

`nvs debug to-test <trace-id>` reads a recorded request and its response from the debug service's
index and prints a test: one class with one `#[Test]` method that sends the same request through
`Core\Test::request` ([`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request)) and asserts what the program answered. The
request is the method, the path and query, the headers and the body the spool recorded. The text goes
through `nvs fmt`'s printer, so it is already formatted. `--write <file>` writes it to a new file and
never replaces one. The viewer's button calls the same function.

**The test asserts the response.** The user decided this. The method asserts the status, the key
headers and the body. The key headers are `Content-Type`, and `Location` when the status is a
redirect: the headers the handler chose, not ones that change with every request. A JSON body is read
through the response's `json()` and compared structurally, so key order and spacing do not fail it.
Any other body is compared as bytes. The spool cuts a response body at `[limits] request_body`
([`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced)), and a test made from a
cut body asserts the status and the key headers only.

A header the record holds as `[redacted]` is written with the string `'redacted'`, and a comment above
it says to put a test credential there. The test compiles as printed, and a route that checks the
credential fails until the developer replaces it. The credential never reaches the test, because it
never reached the spool. A request whose recorded request body is not the whole body is refused, with
the reason: sending part of a body would test a different request.

The test passes against the program that answered the request, and fails when its handler answers with
another status, another key header or another body.

- **Memory:** development only. One request record is read per command.

**Declined:**
- **Copying the credential into the test.** A test is committed, and a credential in it is published.
- **Asserting every response header.** `Date`, a request id and a cookie change with every request, so
  the test would fail against the program that passed it.

<sub>See also [`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request), [`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced), [`testing/the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact`](testing.md#testing-the-viewer-shows-the-stream-and-hands-off-every-artifact).</sub>

<a id="testing-bench-counters"></a>

## `#[Bench]` reports counted semantic work, and CI may gate on the counts but never on wall-clock

`rule:testing/bench-counters`

`#[Bench]` reports counted semantic work — statements executed, calls made, allocations, bytes
attributed, GC cycles — read off the same probe sites coverage and tracing use, in a counting mode
beside their timing one ([`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes)). Those numbers are **bit-identical across
machines, operating systems and architectures**, because they count what the program did rather than
what a CPU did. `bytes` costs no new instrument: memory is already attributable to a request under
an enforceable cap, and this reads that accounting.

CI may gate on the exact rows. It may not gate on wall-clock, which is printed beside them and
labelled advisory on every run.

**A bench is test code that runs only under `nvs test --bench`.** `#[Bench]` (`Core\Test\Bench`)
marks a method of the shape `#[Test]` gives one, in a class `nvs test` discovers, so a bench takes
fixtures, the constructor as setup, hooks and inheritance as a test does, and a build leaves it out
([`testing/tests-never-reach-a-build`](testing.md#testing-tests-never-reach-a-build)). It takes `skip` and `because`, at the types
`#[Test]`'s roster gives them, and no data row. A plain `nvs test` runs no bench and does not count
one as left out; `--bench` runs every bench and no test, one at a time, each once. A bench passes
with no assertion, because what it claims is its rows, and an assertion that fails still fails it.
Why once: its counts are the same on every run, so a repeat or iteration option buys nothing
(simplicity).

The rows are the bench's object and call, counted on its own isolate: the constructor is the
bench's setup and is counted with it, and setup that must not count goes in a `#[Fixture]`, which
is built before the isolate. The thread's empty array is made before the window opens, so a bench's
rows do not depend on which benches ran before it. A bench takes no `seed` or `at`, so one that
reads the clock or `Core\Random` may count differently on each run. A task
the bench spawns counts on a context of its own, which the rows do not include, as `nvs run
--count`'s do not. The text report prints them as `nvs run --count` does, under the bench's line,
and the JSON report gives each bench `counts` and `advisoryWallMs` ([`testing/report-formats`](testing.md#testing-report-formats)).

The counters are comparable across machines and **not** across releases: an optimising tier
eliminates work, so one program's statement count falls between them. "Did my algorithm improve" is
this rule's question; "did Novis get faster" is [`testing/perf-two-mechanisms`](testing.md#testing-perf-two-mechanisms)'s, and the two do
not overlap. There is no per-member cost table and there will not be one — a hand-written claim
about what a `Core` member costs is a number with no guard test.

`nvs run --count` prints the same rows at exit, `gc=` last on the line (`DebugFlags::COUNT` in
`crates/nvs-runtime/src/ctx/mod.rs`, the line in `crates/nvs-cli/src/main.rs`). A GC cycle is one run of
the in-flight collector, counted in `Ctx::collect_if_asked`. The attribute's options are
`crates/nvs-types/src/testing.rs`'s `BENCH_OPTIONS`, and a bench's rows are
`crates/nvs-cli/src/runner.rs`'s `Rows`.

**Declined:**
- **Wall-clock benchmarks with statistical treatment.** It is what other languages ship, and it
  produces a number CI cannot gate on. The counters cost less and produce one it can.
- **Instruction counts under callgrind.** They are Linux-only, many times slower than a plain run
  and blind to symbols inside JIT frames, so a user benchmarking on Windows has none
  ([`testing/perf-two-mechanisms`](testing.md#testing-perf-two-mechanisms) keeps them for measuring Novis itself).
- **A declared per-member cost table.** It would be more faithful for code that spends its time in
  native members, at the price of hundreds of hand-written numbers, none of them guarded.

<sub>See also [`testing/debug-probes`](testing.md#testing-debug-probes), [`testing/perf-two-mechanisms`](testing.md#testing-perf-two-mechanisms), [`testing/member-perf-ledger`](testing.md#testing-member-perf-ledger).</sub>

<a id="testing-perf-two-mechanisms"></a>

## A per-PR guard and the historical dashboard are separate measurements, and never one

`rule:testing/perf-two-mechanisms`

Two performance measurements exist and they are never one.

The **per-PR regression guards** are self-relative wall-clock ratios and slopes — a deep chain
against a shallow one, a throw against a return — and the counts beside them. They run on every
platform, and on a push when the diff touched a crate whose cost they measure. Each comparison
happens on one machine in one run, so it needs no cross-machine comparability, but load on that
machine still moves it. So a timing has two bounds: missing the **soft** one prints a warning into
the CI log and fails nothing, and only the **hard** one, an order of magnitude further or just short
of the change of kind it guards, fails, after re-measuring. A count has one bound and fails at once.
They answer "did this commit regress".

A timing past its hard bound is measured again, up to three attempts, and only the last attempt is
judged: a burst of load that lands on one attempt passes on the next, and a change of kind is past
the bound on every attempt. The soft-bound warning is written straight to standard output, because
libtest holds back what a passing test prints; on GitHub Actions it is a `::warning` command, which
lists it among the run's annotations, and a line in the file `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` names. Each
attempt sits between two readings of a yardstick, a fixed scalar loop, and is labelled `noisy` when
they differ by more than 25% of the faster one and `steady` otherwise; every printed time gives its
ratio to the yardstick. Neither label nor ratio is judged: they are what a reader of a warning has
for telling a busy machine from a slower program. Each test binary carries its own `judge`, so a
change to how a timing is judged is made in `perf_guards.rs`, in the LSP's `latency.rs` and in
`nvs-cli`'s `testing.rs`, whose `judge_margin` judges that binary's `…_by_the_margin_this_test_names`
ratios.

Allocations, emitted calls and executed statements read the same on any machine however loaded, so
where a guard's question can be asked as a count, the count is the check that fails and a timing
beside it is a sanity bound. No counter goes on a production path for a test: a test counts with
a wrapper it supplies, such as a counting `Read` under a stream, or with a `cfg(test)` counter in the
crate whose own tests read it. Where neither reaches, as with `nvs_host::counts`, the counter exists
under `debug_assertions` only, and the release binary has none. A slowdown between the two bounds no longer fails CI, and one with no
count behind it, such as a layout that misses the cache more often, shows only as a warning until it
reaches the hard bound; catching it is the job of a same-machine comparison and of the counts. A
warning is answered by measuring the commit before it on the machine that warned.

**Memory:** none per request or per task; this is test code. A test run pays two yardstick readings
per attempt, and up to two further attempts when a figure is past its hard bound.

The **historical dashboard** compiles a fixed workload on a dedicated, non-shared Linux or WSL
runner and records the aggregate retired-instruction count under callgrind. It answers "is Novis's
own implementation getting faster, in a sense comparable across whoever's machine produced each
point". The instruction count is the headline because it is bit-for-bit reproducible regardless of
CPU generation, thermal state or scheduler; a timer is not, and no cross-machine claim is ever made
from one.

Benchmarking an Novis **program's** own code is neither of these — that is [`testing/bench-counters`](testing.md#testing-bench-counters).

The dashboard's runner is one more piece of infrastructure to keep alive. That cost is accepted,
because the guards cannot answer its question: a self-relative ratio says whether a commit regressed
against itself, never whether Novis got faster in an absolute sense.

**Declined:**
- **One bound per timing.** A bound chosen on one machine is enforced on every other, and load moves
  a figure inside one run, so a single bound is either loose enough to pass the change of kind the
  guard exists for or tight enough to fail with no change behind it.
- **Counting VM opcodes or dispatch-loop iterations.** There is no interpreter tier to count.
- **The hardware's instructions-retired counter** (`perf`, ETW, Instruments). It is locked to one
  architecture and is a different tool on each OS, so it compares across machines of one
  architecture and never across operating systems. Callgrind's emulated instruction stream has
  neither limit.
- **A fixed reference workload, such as a SHA-256 or matrix loop, timed on every machine.** The
  guards' same-run ratios already normalize more simply for regressions, and the instruction count
  is more precise for the trend with no extra reference binary to keep.
- **Callgrind as the gate on every pull request.** Its emulation is one to two orders of magnitude
  slower, which every pull request would pay, and it runs on only one of the three CI platforms.

<sub>See also [`testing/bench-counters`](testing.md#testing-bench-counters), [`testing/member-perf-ledger`](testing.md#testing-member-perf-ledger).</sub>

<a id="testing-member-perf-ledger"></a>

## A member's record is four counts that compare on any machine and one clock that compares on its own, re-measured only when its implementing file's code moves

`rule:testing/member-perf-ledger`

A member's record is four counts and one clock, taken in one sweep over one bench program. The
counts — statements executed, calls made, allocations, bytes, each per operation — are what the
